t.walter sisulu square@-26.3,27.9:
On 26 June 1955, some three thousand delegates gathered on a dusty open field in Kliptown, one of the oldest settlements of what became Soweto, for the Congress of the People. Police surrounded the meeting on its second day, but not before the crowd had adopted the Freedom Charter, the document that opens with the words that South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white. Its ideas went on to shape the country's post-apartheid constitution. The field is now Walter Sisulu Square, named after the anti-apartheid leader and mentor of Nelson Mandela, and the charter's clauses are carved into stone around a monument at its centre.

The square is a big, open civic space, with a conical brick tower, markets and a hotel, and it can feel a little empty on a quiet weekday. Its value lies in what happened here and in what surrounds it. Kliptown itself remains poor, with informal housing close by, and the contrast between monument and neighbourhood is part of the lesson.

A short ride away, in Orlando West, Vilakazi Street is the only street in the world where two Nobel Peace Prize winners lived, Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Mandela's old house is a museum. Nearby, the Hector Pieterson Memorial marks the student uprising of 16 June 1976, when police opened fire on schoolchildren protesting against being taught in Afrikaans. It is a powerful, sobering place.

Riding in Johannesburg is about traffic and awareness rather than scenery. Roads are wide and fast, but minibus taxis stop and swerve without warning, potholes appear suddenly, and traffic lights, known locally as robots, are often out of action during power cuts. The city sits high on the Highveld at around seventeen hundred metres, and summer afternoons bring violent thunderstorms with hail, while winter days are dry, sunny and cold in the mornings. Personal security is a real concern: ride in daylight, keep your bike in sight or in guarded parking, and consider visiting Soweto with a local guide, which also makes the experience much richer.

Fuel is everywhere in Soweto and Johannesburg, with attendants filling the tank for you. For lunch try a kota, a quarter-loaf of bread stuffed with chips, sauce and meat, or grilled meat at a shisa nyama, eaten outside with friends and loud music.
t.liliesleaf@-26.0,28.1:
In the early 1960s, Rivonia was a quiet farming area on the northern edge of Johannesburg, and Liliesleaf was a smallholding with a farmhouse, outbuildings and a thatched cottage. It was bought, through a front, by the South African Communist Party and used as a secret headquarters by the leadership of the liberation movement, including Umkhonto we Sizwe, the armed wing of the African National Congress. Nelson Mandela lived here for a time under a false name, posing as a worker called David Motsamayi. On 11 July 1963, police raided the farm and arrested much of the leadership, seizing documents that led to the Rivonia Trial, in which Mandela and others were sentenced to life imprisonment. Mandela's speech from the dock, declaring an ideal for which he was prepared to die, became one of the defining moments of the struggle against apartheid.

Liliesleaf is now a museum and heritage site, with exhibits telling the story of the raid, the trial and the wider struggle. In 2024, it became part of the UNESCO World Heritage site Human Rights, Liberation and Reconciliation: Nelson Mandela Legacy Sites. The once-rural farm is now surrounded by the affluent northern suburbs of Johannesburg, with walls, security gates and busy roads, a stark contrast with the secret life it once hid.

The riding in Johannesburg's northern suburbs is urban, with heavy traffic, traffic lights, minibus taxis and potholes. Personal security is a concern, so ride in daylight, keep valuables out of sight and park in secure areas. For better riding, head north-west towards the Cradle of Humankind, a World Heritage site of caves where some of the most important early human fossils have been found, including at Sterkfontein. The roads through the rolling grasslands and hills of the Magaliesberg, towards the Hartbeespoort dam, are popular with local riders, with curves, climbs and views.

The Highveld climate is pleasant for much of the year, with sunny days and cool nights, though summer afternoons bring dramatic thunderstorms with lightning and hail. Winter mornings can be cold.

Fuel, food and every service are easy to find in Randburg, Sandton and the surrounding suburbs. Try boerewors, a spiced sausage grilled on the braai, or a plate of pap and chakalaka, a maize porridge with spicy relish, at a local restaurant.
t.sterkfontein@-25.9,27.8:
Some of the most important clues to human evolution have come out of a set of limestone caves in the grassland north-west of Johannesburg. The Sterkfontein caves, in the area known as the Cradle of Humankind, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, have yielded hundreds of hominin fossils, including Mrs Ples, a skull of Australopithecus africanus about two million years old, found in 1947, and Little Foot, an almost complete skeleton of an Australopithecus, painstakingly extracted from the rock over two decades.

The caves were mined for lime in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and the miners blasted out fossils with the rock. Scientists began systematic work here in the 1930s, and excavations continue today. Guided tours take visitors into the caves, through chambers and passages, and explain what was found where. Maropeng, a visitor centre nearby, presents the story of human evolution in an engaging way, with exhibitions and a boat ride through the elements.

The riding around the Cradle of Humankind is pleasant, with roads winding through the rolling grassland of the Highveld, dotted with farms, game reserves and small towns. The Magaliesberg mountains, to the north, offer more winding roads and fine views. Traffic near Johannesburg can be heavy, and driving is on the left. Summer, from October to March, brings afternoon thunderstorms, sometimes violent, with hail, and the winter is dry and sunny, with cold nights. Be aware of security: keep your bike and belongings secure, and avoid riding at night in unfamiliar areas.

Muldersdrift and Krugersdorp, nearby, have fuel, shops and restaurants, and Johannesburg has all services. The area has many lodges, restaurants and farm stalls, popular with weekend visitors from the city. South African food includes braai, barbecue, boerewors, a spiced sausage, and biltong, dried meat, perfect for a ride. Visiting the caves, and seeing the place where our ancestors' bones lay for millions of years, is a humbling experience.
t.coal mines historic site@-43.0,147.7:
The worst convicts in Van Diemen's Land were sent to Port Arthur, and the worst of those were sent here. The Coal Mines on the Tasman Peninsula, in southeastern Tasmania, were established in the 1830s to supply coal to the colony and to punish repeat offenders with hard labour underground. Men worked in dark, damp shafts and tunnels, hauling coal in terrible conditions, and solitary cells were built for those who broke the rules. The site was closed in the 1840s, and today the ruins of the barracks, cells, chapel and mine shafts lie scattered among the eucalyptus forest beside the sea. It is one of eleven places that make up the Australian Convict Sites World Heritage property, listed in 2010.

The Coal Mines are much quieter than Port Arthur, which draws coaches and crowds. Here you can wander alone among the ruins, listening to the birds and the waves, reading the stories on the information boards. The setting is beautiful, with views across Norfolk Bay, and the contrast between the peaceful landscape and its history is striking.

The Tasman Peninsula is connected to the rest of Tasmania by a narrow isthmus at Eaglehawk Neck, which the convict authorities guarded with a line of chained dogs to stop escapes. The coast around it has dramatic cliffs, sea caves and rock formations, including the Tessellated Pavement, a flat rock shelf cracked into rectangular tiles, and the Tasman Arch and Devils Kitchen. Port Arthur, on the southern side of the peninsula, is well worth a visit.

The riding is excellent. The Arthur Highway from Hobart winds through farmland and forest, along the coast and over hills, with good surfaces and plenty of bends. The minor roads on the peninsula are narrower and quieter, some of them gravel. Watch for wildlife: wallabies, pademelons, possums and wombats are common on the roads, especially at dawn and dusk, and hitting one can be dangerous. Weather in Tasmania changes quickly, with rain, wind and cold possible at any time of year.

The nearest towns with services are Nubeena, on the peninsula, and Sorell or Dunalley on the way from Hobart. Fuel is available in these towns, but stations are few and far between, so fill up when you can. Try the local seafood: oysters, scallops and fish from these waters are excellent.
t.meschkanzi meskonys@54.9,25.3:
In a field near the village of Meškonys, north of Vilnius, a small stone marker records one of the most patient scientific projects of the nineteenth century. Between 1816 and 1855, the astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve and his colleagues measured a chain of triangles running from Hammerfest on the Arctic coast of Norway to the Black Sea, nearly three thousand kilometres, to determine the exact size and shape of the Earth. Meškonys, written as Meschkanzi in the old survey records, was one of the stations, and it is one of the points of the Struve Geodetic Arc, inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2005 across ten countries.

There is not much to see: a marker, an information board, perhaps a few flowers. What matters is the idea. Surveyors climbed towers and hills with heavy instruments, sighting from one station to the next through all weathers, and calculated the curvature of the planet with astonishing precision. The arc helped show that the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, and it laid the foundations for modern mapping.

The countryside around Meškonys is classic eastern Lithuania: gentle hills, pine and birch forests, small lakes, fields of grain and scattered farmsteads. The Neris river winds through the landscape, and storks nest on poles and rooftops in summer. It is a quiet, peaceful area, with little traffic and a slow pace of life.

Riding here is relaxed. Roads are mostly flat or gently rolling, with long straights through forests and farmland. Surfaces vary, from good asphalt on main roads to gravel on smaller ones. Kernavė, the medieval capital of Lithuania, with its hill forts above the Neris, is a short ride west and another World Heritage Site. Vilnius, with its baroque old town, is close enough for a day trip.

Nemenčinė, thirteen kilometres away, has fuel and shops. Lithuanian food is hearty: cepelinai, big potato dumplings stuffed with meat and topped with sour cream and bacon, and šaltibarščiai, a cold pink beetroot soup that is perfect on a hot summer day. Winters are cold and snowy, and the riding season runs from about May to September.
t.sharpeville graves site a@-26.7,27.9:
On 21 March 1960, a crowd of several thousand people gathered at the police station in Sharpeville, a township south of Johannesburg, to protest against the pass laws, which forced Black South Africans to carry documents and restricted their movement. The police opened fire. Sixty-nine people were killed, many of them shot in the back as they ran, and many more were wounded. The massacre became a turning point: it brought the apartheid regime worldwide condemnation, led to the banning of the African National Congress and the Pan Africanist Congress, and pushed the liberation movement towards armed struggle. Today, 21 March is a public holiday, Human Rights Day.

The graves of many of the victims lie in the cemetery in the Phelindaba section of the township, and they have been preserved as a memorial site, part of the group of Nelson Mandela legacy sites that UNESCO listed in 2024 under the heading of human rights, liberation struggle and reconciliation. It is a quiet and solemn place, with rows of simple headstones, and the memorial and exhibition by the old police station nearby tell the story in photographs and testimony. A local guide, ideally someone from Sharpeville, makes an enormous difference to the experience. Visit respectfully, ask before taking photographs, and take your time.

The setting is the industrial Vaal Triangle, a region of steelworks, power stations and sprawling townships on the Vaal river, with Vereeniging and Vanderbijlpark the two main towns. Vereeniging has its own history: the treaty that ended the South African War in 1902 was signed here. Riding in this area means highway riding on the Highveld, a high, flat grassland at about 1,500 metres, where the air is thin and clear, the sky is huge and summer afternoons bring spectacular thunderstorms. Winter days are dry and sunny, though nights can be near freezing. Take care with traffic, taxi minibuses and potholes.

Fuel and food are easy in Vereeniging and Vanderbijlpark, only a few kilometres away, and there are shopping centres and restaurants of every kind. Like any large South African urban area, the Vaal requires sensible precautions with security, so keep valuables out of sight, avoid riding at night, and ask your guide about the areas to avoid.
t.beresnaki paliepiukai@54.6,25.4:
The Neris is the river that winds out of the hills of eastern Lithuania and runs through Vilnius, and just upstream of the capital it flows through a landscape of pine forest, sandy terraces and soft green valleys. This is the country of Kernave, a village of a few hundred people that was, in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, one of the main centres of the Lithuanian state. Five hillforts rise above the river valley here, together with the traces of an old town on the flat ground below, and the whole archaeological site was listed by UNESCO in 2004. The label of Beresnaki and Paliepiukai sits along the same valley, and its villages belong to the same countryside.

Kernave was a pagan capital, the seat of grand dukes before Vilnius took over, and it was burned by the Teutonic Order in 1390 during the long wars between the Order and Lithuania. The hillforts, topped now with grass and looking like huge green loaves, were the defences, and the town below was a trading place. Excavations have found hundreds of thousands of objects, from jewellery to weapons and tools, and there is a museum where you can see them. In summer, a festival of living archaeology fills the area with people in medieval dress, who demonstrate crafts and combat, and the atmosphere is lively. The other ride title, Modernist Kaunas, is a different kind of heritage altogether, a city of interwar architecture.

For a rider, this is gentle, green and quiet. The roads in the Neris valley wind among fields and forest, with moderate bends, smooth tarmac and very little traffic outside Vilnius. In midsummer, the light lasts until late in the evening, and the white nights are a joy. Wind, rain and sudden cold snaps are possible at any time, and winters are cold and snowy. The best months are May to September.

Skaidiskes and Rasos, the nearest places, have shops and petrol stations, and Vilnius is only a short ride away, with all the services. Try cepelinai, the potato dumplings stuffed with meat, and a cold beetroot soup in summer, and the dark rye bread of the region. Bring insect repellent, because the mosquitoes in the forests can be fierce.
t.tasmanian wilderness@-43.1,146.2:
At this latitude, almost the whole of the southwest corner of Tasmania is wilderness in the strict sense: no towns, almost no roads, and a climate that comes straight from the Southern Ocean. The Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area covers a fifth of the island and includes button-grass plains, glacier-carved valleys, rainforest and the long white quartzite ranges.

You do not ride into this country so much as up to the edge of it. The Southwest National Park is mostly reachable on foot, by boat or by light aircraft, and the roads that come nearest, the one down the Huon to Cockle Creek and the Gordon River road in the west, both end a long way from Hobart. The surface is mostly sealed, with winding sections through the Huon Valley, apple country, and tall forest of eucalypts such as swamp gum, among the tallest flowering trees on earth.

The weather is the main character. Tasmania's west and south get the Roaring Forties, and rain, wind and sudden cold can arrive on any day of the year. A clear morning can be followed by hail by lunchtime. Pack proper waterproofs and warm layers even in summer, and give yourself time, because roads here are twisty and slow. Wildlife on the road is real: wallabies, pademelons and wombats come out at dusk, and the Tasmanian devil, once common, is now rare enough that seeing one is an event. Slow down at the edges of the day.

Fuel is the thing you must plan. Do not assume anything in the wilderness itself, and the roads that approach it are far from this exact point. Huonville and Geeveston, in the Huon Valley, are the larger stops on the way south, and you should fill up before heading to the end of the road. Some people also carry a spare bottle of water and a snack. The Huon and the D'Entrecasteaux Channel are also known for fresh seafood, particularly salmon, scallops and oysters, so a late lunch at one of the waterside places is a good idea. Summer, from December to February, gives the longest days and the most stable weather, though stable is relative. The reward is a view across a huge, empty, deeply green landscape.
t.mir castle complex@53.5,26.5:
Mir Castle looks like it belongs in a fairy tale, though the people who owned it were serious and sometimes violent. Work began in the early sixteenth century for the Ilinich family, in a Gothic style with corner towers and brick walls, and the castle passed to the powerful Radziwiłł family, who added Renaissance and Baroque touches, ramparts and a park with a pond. Today it stands in the small town of Mir in western Belarus, which has only about 2,500 people, and the whole complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The castle has had a hard life. It was damaged in the wars that swept the region in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, left in ruins for a long time and used by the Nazis as part of a ghetto in the Second World War, when many local Jews were held there before being killed. After the war it was restored, and it now houses a museum. The red brick, the turrets and the reflection in the moat make a strong picture, especially in the soft light of early morning.

The ride across this part of Belarus is flat and calm. Roads are generally well surfaced and the landscape is a mix of fields, birch and pine woods and small villages with painted wooden houses. Traffic is light outside the larger towns, and there are cameras and police checks, so keep to the speed limits. Autumn colour is lovely, while winter can bring snow and ice. Before you go, check current entry rules, insurance and border conditions for your passport, as these have changed repeatedly and visas, registration and road tolls may apply.

Mir is small, and the nearest bigger town with a full range of shops and fuel is Stowbtsy, about 18 km away, while Navahrudak, a historic town linked to Adam Mickiewicz, is a worthwhile detour for a ride. Cafés near the castle serve local dishes such as draniki, potato pancakes with sour cream, and dishes made with mushrooms, pork and dill. Pause for a walk around the moat and the park, and allow a couple of hours if you want to see the inside of the castle. The villages around hold a quiet, rural character.
t.sharpeville massacre site police station:
Sharpeville is a heavy place, and it should be approached quietly. On 21 March 1960, thousands of people gathered outside the police station to protest against the pass laws, which forced Black South Africans to carry documents controlling where they could live and work. The police opened fire on the crowd, and sixty-nine people were killed, many shot in the back as they fled. The massacre shocked the world, led to the banning of liberation movements in South Africa and hardened international opposition to apartheid.

The police station still stands, and the Sharpeville precinct now includes a memorial, a human rights exhibition and the graves of victims, all part of a heritage route. In 1996, Nelson Mandela signed South Africa's new constitution into law in Sharpeville, a choice that carried deliberate meaning. The sites were included in UNESCO's listing of places associated with Mandela's legacy, and 21 March is now a public holiday known as Human Rights Day.

The place lies on the southern edge of Gauteng, beside the twin cities of Vereeniging and Vanderbijlpark, where the Vaal river runs and heavy industry spreads for miles. Riding here means highways, trucks and urban traffic. The N1 and the roads from Johannesburg are fast and busy, and local roads can have potholes. Fuel, food and everything else you need are easy to find in Vanderbijlpark and Vereeniging, both close and large.

Be careful and sensible, as you would in any big South African city. Park where you can see the bike, travel in daylight, and consider going with a local guide, who can explain the story and open doors that would otherwise stay closed. Winter days are dry and clear, with cold mornings, while summer brings afternoon thunderstorms. Visit in a respectful frame of mind, take your helmet off, and give yourself time to read the names. This is not a stop for a quick photo.
t.union buildings@-25.7,28.2:
Pretoria's Union Buildings stand on Meintjieskop, a ridge above the city, and the view from the terraces carries all the way down to Church Square and out to the hills beyond. Sir Herbert Baker designed the complex, which was finished in 1913 as the seat of government of the newly formed Union of South Africa. Two wings join in a sweeping colonnaded curve, built in pale sandstone, and the formal gardens climb the slope in terraces.

The building has done double duty as a symbol. It was the centre of white minority rule, then, in May 1994, the place where Nelson Mandela was inaugurated as president, with crowds on the lawns and military aircraft overhead. A large bronze statue of Mandela now stands in the gardens with arms outstretched, and the buildings figure in the UNESCO listing of places connected to his legacy. The contrast between the two stories is part of why it is worth seeing.

In October, Pretoria turns purple, because jacaranda trees line the streets by the thousand and bloom together. That is the best moment to ride here, because the avenues of Brooklyn, Arcadia and Hatfield are dusted with fallen flowers. The city is a good motorcycle town in daylight, with wide roads, mild winters and reliable weather, though traffic can be heavy and drivers fast. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms that arrive with little warning and can flood underpasses.

Pretoria is large, with about one and a half million people in the city proper, and fuel, food, repairs and hotels are plentiful, with Centurion to the south as another big hub. Parking near the Union Buildings is possible, but security guards may direct you. Take your time, walk up the gardens and look at the Voortrekker Monument on its hill across the valley, which tells a very different story about the same city. Pretoria rewards slow looking at both.
t.vilnius@54.7,25.3:
Vilnius is a city that takes a few hours to like and a few days to love. The old town, one of the largest surviving medieval centres in Eastern Europe, is a tangle of cobbled lanes and courtyards on the banks of the Neris and Vilnia rivers, and it is crowded with churches, more than forty of them by most counts, in Gothic, Renaissance and especially Baroque styles. From the top of Gediminas Hill you see red roofs, green domes and the dark line of forest beyond.

The city's story is a layered one. It became the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the fourteenth century, then lived under Polish, Russian, Nazi and Soviet rule, and each left traces. Vilnius was once a major centre of Jewish life, known as the Jerusalem of the North, and the old Jewish quarter still marks that history. University buildings from the sixteenth century sit near the cathedral, and Užupis, a bohemian district across the river, declares itself an independent republic every April Fool's Day, with its own constitution on a wall.

As a start for a ride toward the Aukštaitija lakes, the city is a good launch pad. You leave through suburbs, then roads open into forest and farmland, with long straight stretches, gentle hills and lakes shining between pines. Surfaces are generally good, and drivers are brisk but not wild. Summer is warm and bright, with very long evenings, and autumn brings colour. Winter can be icy.

Everything you could need is here. Fuel is on every approach road, hotels and guesthouses cover all budgets, and the food is hearty. Try cepelinai, the big potato dumplings stuffed with meat, or cold beetroot soup in summer, with a glass of local kvass. Old-town parking can be awkward, so leave the bike at a hotel and walk. A free hour near the cathedral square is enough for the first look.
t.hobart@-42.9,147.3:
Hobart tucks itself against the foot of Mount Wellington, with the wide Derwent estuary at its feet, and it has the compact, sandstone-and-timber feel of a port that never grew too large. It is the capital of Tasmania and Australia's second oldest city, founded in 1804 as a convict settlement, and the old warehouses along Salamanca Place and the cottages of Battery Point survive from the early years of the colony. On Saturdays, Salamanca Place fills with a crowded market of stalls selling food, crafts and plants.

The sea defines the town. Each year, ocean racing yachts finish the Sydney to Hobart race in the harbour on or around 27 December, and crowds gather at Constitution Dock to cheer them in. The Museum of Old and New Art, MONA, on a peninsula up the river, has put the city on the international arts map with a bold underground gallery, and is reached by ferry. Mount Wellington, at about 1,270 metres, often carries snow even in summer, and a narrow road climbs to a lookout with views over the whole river.

The ride east begins with a crossing of the Tasman Bridge, then follows the Tasman and Tasman Highway through Sorell, Orford and Triabunna, with the coast of the Tasman Sea opening up. The Great Eastern Drive continues to Swansea, with stretches of bays, white beaches and low hills, and then up toward Freycinet Peninsula, famous for the granite peaks called the Hazards and Wineglass Bay. The roads are well maintained, with smooth bends and limited traffic outside school holidays. Wildlife, especially wallabies and wombats, is a real hazard at dawn and dusk. Weather changes quickly, so carry layers even in summer.

Hobart has everything: fuel stations, supermarkets, workshops and accommodation. Fuel is available in towns along the east coast, though they are some distance apart, so fill up when you can. Try fresh scallops, oysters or fish and chips from a floating shop on the harbour, and local cool-climate wines and whisky. Book accommodation ahead in January, when the city is busy.
t.darlington probation station@-42.6,148.1:
Maria Island lies just off Tasmania's east coast, and Darlington is the little settlement on its sheltered north-western shore where convicts, officials and later Italian entrepreneurs left their mark. No cars are allowed on the island and no one lives there permanently, so what you find is a quiet bay, a scatter of Georgian buildings and a lot of wildlife. You reach it by passenger ferry from Triabunna on the mainland, and the crossing takes about half an hour.

The settlement began in the 1820s as a penal colony for convicts who had reoffended in the colony, and the surviving buildings date from several phases. The probation station phase, in the 1840s, was part of the British system of reform through labour and separation, and the brick barracks, the commissariat store and the cottages are among the buildings that make up the Australian Convict Sites World Heritage listing. Later, in the 1880s, an Italian businessman, Diego Bernacchi, tried to turn the island into a centre of silk, wine and cement, and his plans left behind an old cement works and a few historic houses before failing.

The island's wildlife is the real show. Forester kangaroos, Bennett's wallabies and wombats graze on the grass around Darlington, often entirely unbothered by visitors, and Tasmanian devils were reintroduced to the island in 2012 as an insurance population. The Painted Cliffs, sandstone formations striped by iron minerals, are a short walk along the shore at low tide. Rides here are on foot or by bicycle, since the island is car-free, along gravel tracks that lead to the Fossil Cliffs and up Bishop and Clerk, a rocky peak.

Park the motorcycle at Triabunna, where the town has fuel and cafes, and book the ferry in advance in summer. Wind and sea conditions can cancel sailings, and the weather changes quickly, so carry waterproofs.
t.vredefort dome core area@-26.9,27.3:
Two billion years ago, give or take, something the size of a mountain hit the Earth here at astonishing speed. The Vredefort Dome is what survives of the biggest verified impact structure on the planet, and also one of the oldest. The original crater is estimated to have been around three hundred kilometres across, and erosion has since scraped away most of its form, leaving a ring of low hills about seventy kilometres wide around an uplifted core. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 2005, which sounds dry until you stand on the rim and realise that the whole arrangement of rock beneath your tyres was thrown up in minutes.

From the saddle you will not see a crater, and that is part of the point. Vredefort is about understanding rather than seeing. Granite from deep in the crust was pushed to the surface at the centre, and around it the rocks are tilted on end in great arcs. Geologists find shattered cones, a rock fabric that forms only under extreme pressure, and in the landscape the effect is a ring of quartzite ridges around gentle farmland. The Vaal river wanders through the area, and the town of Parys on its banks is the usual base.

The riding here is relaxed and pleasant rather than dramatic. Secondary roads run through maize farms and low koppies, mostly in good condition although with the odd pothole, and traffic is light except at weekends when Johannesburg bikers come out to Parys. The best months are April to June and September to October, when the days are warm and dry, and the veld is golden or fresh green. Summer brings afternoon thunderstorms that can be violent, with hail and lightning.

Parys and Vredefort both sell fuel, and Parys has plenty of cafés and guesthouses, plus a long-standing reputation as an arts town. The area is rich in birdlife, and wildlife includes antelope, and the Vaal draws kayakers and anglers. The gold of the Witwatersrand, which made Johannesburg, lies in rocks that the impact helped to preserve, so the crater is distantly linked to the wealth of the whole country. Pack water, a sun hat and a taste for big skies.
t.freycinet@-42.1,148.3:
Freycinet is the peninsula on Tasmania's east coast where a granite spine called the Hazards rises pink and orange out of the sea, the kind of rock that looks stained by the last sunset, and the colour comes from the feldspar in the stone. The famous curve of Wineglass Bay lies on the far side, a white arc of sand reached by a steep walking track of about an hour from the car park, and a good viewpoint is on the way up; it is a fair climb in motorcycle boots, so plan to change shoes.

The drive in is the Great Eastern Drive, about 170 kilometres along the coast from Orford in the south to St Helens in the north. From Hobart you take the Tasman Highway through the Sorell and Orford area, then run north with the sea on one side and low hills on the other, past Triabunna, where the ferry leaves for Maria Island, and through the small seaside town of Swansea, where a wide bay faces the Hazards across the water. The corners are gentle and the road is generally good, with a couple of climbs through forest, and the traffic is light compared with the mainland.

At the peninsula itself, the national park takes an entry fee, and Coles Bay is the little settlement at the gate, with a shop and a few places to eat, including local oysters from the nearby farms, which are among the best you will find.

Wildlife is the hazard and the delight. Wallabies and pademelons graze by the roadside at dusk and dawn, and wombats and the occasional Tasmanian devil are killed on the roads at night, so avoid riding after dark if you can. The weather is changeable, with cold southerlies from the Southern Ocean, but a clear morning here is as good as it gets.
t.orford@-42.6,147.9:
Orford is a small seaside town on the east coast of Tasmania, at the mouth of the Prosser River, and it has the easygoing feel of a place that has always been a bit off the main road. The river runs through a pretty valley and into a sheltered bay, where fishing boats and kayaks bob in the water and walkers follow a path along the bank. Across the water lies Maria Island, a national park with no cars, where wombats, Forester kangaroos and Tasmanian devils roam among ruins of a convict settlement and a short-lived cement works.

The ferry to Maria Island leaves from nearby Triabunna, about ten kilometres up the coast, and the island is a rewarding day trip if you are not in a hurry. Visitors are welcome in some areas, though a motorcyclist should check what is open before riding off the main road. The place names alone, Creole, Grand Chenier, Little Chenier, give you a sense of the French heritage that still runs through the language and food.

The riding is flat, straight, and quiet. The road runs between marsh and ridge, with the horizon always visible, and the sky takes up most of what you see. It is not a technical ride, and many people will find it slightly hypnotic. The risks are crosswinds, heavy rain from afternoon storms, and the occasional animal on the road, so keep your speed sensible and your eyes open. In spring and autumn the oaks fill with migrating birds, and the sight of a tree dripping with warblers on a cool morning is something you will remember.

Services are scarce along this part of the route. Cameron, around thirty-six kilometres to the west, is itself small, and the bigger towns of Sulphur and Lake Charles are a long way back. Fill your tank well before you set out, bring plenty of water, and be ready for mosquitoes whenever you stop near the marsh. The best seasons are the cooler ones, and a clear winter day can be lovely. High summer is hot and humid, with the added risk of tropical storms, and the road can flood quickly in a surge.
t.sani pass lower control@-29.6,29.3:
The lower control post is where Sani Pass begins to feel real. You have ridden up from the green foothills of the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg, past farms, pine plantations, and the villages of Himeville and Underberg, and at the end of a quiet road you arrive at a small border post of the South African side, with a barrier, an office, and a view of the great basalt wall that closes off the valley. Beyond it, the road turns to gravel and heads straight at the escarpment.

This is the point of no return, in a sense. You must show your passport and vehicle papers, and the staff will ask where you are going and often check whether your vehicle is suitable. The post is only open during daytime hours and closes in the afternoon, so check the times before you go, and remember that the Lesotho border post at the top has its own rules and visa requirements. Carry your documents in a dry place, and have copies, because mountain weather can be harsh and the process can take time.

The pass itself is gravel and steep, climbing around a thousand metres in only a few kilometres, with tight hairpins, rocky ramps, and stream crossings. It is considered a 4x4 route, and many riders attempt it on adventure bikes, though a heavily laden machine or an inexperienced rider can find it exhausting. The surface changes with the weather, and rain, snow, or ice can make it dangerous. Ride it early, well within your skill, and consider the descent as carefully as the climb.

Fuel and supplies should be arranged in Underberg or Himeville, the last sizeable places on the South African side, where there are stations, shops, and places to eat. There is nothing at the control post, apart from a few basic facilities. Bring warm layers, because it can be cold at the top even in summer, and the weather can change in minutes. Winter snow often closes the pass, and spring and autumn offer the best balance of clear weather and safe conditions. The view up to the wall of the escarpment from here is worth a pause.
t.sani pass@-29.6,29.3:
Sani Pass tops out at 2,876 metres, and the Lesotho side greets you with a wide, windswept plateau and a pub that styles itself as the highest in Africa. The ride up is one of the most famous in southern Africa, a rough gravel track that climbs the Drakensberg escarpment in a series of hairpins, but the arrival is almost an anticlimax: you crest the last rise and the land opens into rolling, treeless highlands, grazed by sheep, goats, and herders in blankets.

Lesotho is a country entirely above one thousand metres, and this part of it is the roof. The Maloti Mountains stretch away in every direction, and Thabana Ntlenyana, the highest peak in southern Africa at around 3,480 metres, lies not far away. The Basotho people who live here wear traditional woollen blankets and conical straw hats, ride ponies, and tend livestock in a landscape that has changed little over generations. The air is thin, the light is very clear, and the cold bites, even in summer.

Riding on the plateau is a different challenge to the pass. The road continues as gravel and dirt toward Mokhotlong, the nearest town, about thirty-nine kilometres away, and conditions vary from smooth to rough. Streams cross the track, and snow or ice can appear at any time of year. Distances are deceptive, and daylight hours matter. Wind can be fierce, and there are few places to shelter. Livestock and people walk on the road, so keep your speed under control and be courteous.

Fuel is the main logistical question. Mokhotlong is the nearest place likely to have it, and supplies can be unreliable, so fill up in Underberg or Himeville before the climb and carry a reserve. Plan your border formalities carefully, since the Lesotho post has its own hours and procedures. The pub and a small lodge at the top offer food, drink, and a bed, and it is an excellent place to warm up with a hot meal. Visibility can drop quickly in cloud, so do not go on without a decent weather window.
t.sani top@-29.6,29.3:
Sani Top is the lip of the Drakensberg escarpment, where the gravel road from KwaZulu-Natal finally scrambles over the wall of the mountains into Lesotho at close to twenty-nine hundred metres. It is the highest road pass in southern Africa, and it is not a casual outing. The track climbs about a thousand metres in eight kilometres or so, in steep hairpins up the face of the escarpment, over loose rock, with sheer drops, and the sensible rider treats it as a serious off-road challenge. Rain or snow can close it, and a gentle morning can turn into a white-out by lunch.

At the top, you find a border post, a few huts, and a lodge that claims the highest pub in Africa. The border is real: you need your passport, vehicle papers and patience, and the South African side closes in the late afternoon, so plan your timing. A hot drink in the pub, with a view over the high plateau of the Maloti Mountains, is a pleasure that is hard to beat after the climb. The air is thin, the wind can be bitter, and in winter snow lies on the ground.

The Sotho people have lived in these mountains for centuries, wearing woollen blankets and conical straw hats, and herding sheep, goats and ponies. Shepherds on horseback are a common sight on the plateau. The rolling highlands are treeless and windswept, grassland and bog, with the headwaters of rivers that feed much of southern Africa. The Drakensberg is a spectacular wall of basalt, and in summer, thunderstorms boil over the peaks in the afternoon, so start early. Birdwatchers look for the bearded vulture and the Cape vulture, and the rare bald ibis.

Fuel is the first question. Fill up at Underberg on the South African side, carry spare if your bike's range is limited, and ask about fuel at Mokhotlong, about forty kilometres into Lesotho, which is the nearest sizeable town on the far side. Cash in local currency or South African rand is useful.

The reward is the silence of the plateau, and the sense of having reached somewhere that most people never see.
t.16 june 1976 the streets of orlando west:
Orlando West looks ordinary at first: tidy brick houses, kids in school uniform, taxis hooting at every corner, smoke from braai stands curling over the street. It is in Soweto, about fifteen kilometres southwest of central Johannesburg, and on the morning of 16 June 1976 these were the streets where thousands of schoolchildren marched against being taught in Afrikaans. Police opened fire. Among the first killed was twelve-year-old Hector Pieterson, and the photograph of him being carried by an older student went around the world.

The Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum stands a few blocks from where he fell, and it is worth an unhurried hour. It walks you through that day minute by minute, with the voices of people who were there, and it explains why the uprising changed the course of apartheid. The day is now a national public holiday, Youth Day. Nearby Vilakazi Street is famous as the only street in the world where two Nobel Peace Prize winners lived, Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu; Mandela's small house is a museum, and the street has cafés and restaurants where you can eat well.

As riding goes, Soweto is city work. Traffic is dense and unpredictable, minibus taxis stop wherever they please, and potholes appear without warning. The approach from the Johannesburg side via the old Potchefstroom road or the motorways is straightforward, and the open highveld beyond, towards Sterkfontein and the Cradle of Humankind, is where you get your reward: long straight roads under huge skies and sudden summer thunderstorms that build every afternoon from about November to March.

Fuel is everywhere, with attendants who fill up for you and expect a small tip. Ride here in daylight, park where you can see the bike or where a car guard is watching, and consider joining a local guide, who will add stories no plaque can tell. Try a kota, a hollowed quarter loaf stuffed with chips, polony and atchar, then sit for a moment at the memorial fountain and let the place settle in.
t.constitution hill@-26.2,28.0:
Constitution Hill sits on a ridge between Braamfontein and Hillbrow in central Johannesburg, and few places in South Africa carry so much history in so small a space. The Old Fort here was built in the 1890s under Paul Kruger's Transvaal Republic, and it soon became a notorious prison. Over the following decades the complex, including the infamous Number Four section for black men and the Women's Jail, held thousands of people, from ordinary criminals to political prisoners. Mahatma Gandhi was detained here in the early twentieth century, and Nelson Mandela was held in the Old Fort in the 1960s.

After apartheid ended, the new democracy made a powerful decision: to build the Constitutional Court, the guardian of the country's new rights-based constitution, right here on the site of the prison. The court building, opened in the 2000s, incorporates bricks from demolished cells, and its entrance doors are carved with the rights of the constitution. The museum in the old cells is powerful and unsettling, telling the stories of prisoners through their own words. Guided tours bring the place to life and are well worth it.

Riding in central Johannesburg is busy and demanding. Traffic is heavy, minibus taxis stop without warning, and traffic lights are sometimes out of action because of power cuts or theft of cables, in which case junctions work as four-way stops. Potholes can be deep, and caution is wise around intersections. The highveld around Johannesburg is high, at around seventeen hundred metres, with crisp, clear winters and summer thunderstorms that often arrive in the late afternoon with spectacular lightning and sometimes hail.

Fuel stations are everywhere, with attendants. Park in secure areas, ideally on site, and stay alert in the surrounding streets, particularly after dark. The neighbourhood of Braamfontein next door has a lively scene of cafés, galleries and student bars, and on weekends markets with food and craft stalls. Try a bunny chow, a hollowed loaf filled with curry, or boerewors from a braai, and take a moment on the hill to look out over the city's towers.
t.sharpeville memorial garden@-26.7,27.9:
On 21 March 1960, a crowd of several thousand people gathered outside the police station in Sharpeville, a township near Vereeniging in the south of Gauteng, to protest against the pass laws, which required black South Africans to carry documents restricting where they could live and work. The police opened fire, killing sixty nine people and wounding many more, most of them shot in the back as they fled. The massacre shocked the world and marked a turning point in the struggle against apartheid, leading to the banning of the liberation movements and the start of armed resistance. The date is now commemorated in South Africa as Human Rights Day, and internationally as the day for the elimination of racial discrimination.

The memorial garden and the exhibition centre stand near the site of the shooting, with a wall bearing the names of those who died and a museum that tells the story of the massacre and its aftermath. It was in Sharpeville, in December 1996, that President Nelson Mandela signed the new constitution of South Africa into law, a powerful symbol of the change the country had undergone. The memorial is part of a group of sites associated with the human rights struggle that was added to the World Heritage list in 2024.

The area around Sharpeville is part of the Vaal Triangle, an industrial region between Vereeniging, Vanderbijlpark and Sasolburg, with steel works, power stations and refineries. The Vaal River, which runs through the area, is a popular spot for boating and fishing, and there are restaurants and resorts along its banks. Riding here is mostly on busy urban and suburban roads, with heavy traffic, trucks and minibus taxis that stop without warning.

Vanderbijlpark and Vereeniging have fuel, shops and restaurants, and Johannesburg is about an hour to the north. To the north west, the Cradle of Humankind, with the fossil caves of Sterkfontein and Maropeng, offers a fascinating day trip, with quieter roads through the grasslands. As in much of South Africa, it is advisable to ride during daylight, keep valuables out of sight, and seek local advice about safe routes. The weather on the Highveld is generally sunny, with summer thunderstorms in the afternoons and cold, dry winters.
t.cascades female factory@-42.9,147.3:
In the shadow of kunanyi, the mountain that rises behind Hobart, a set of high stone walls in South Hobart marks the site of the Cascades Female Factory, where thousands of women convicts transported from Britain and Ireland were held in the nineteenth century. They worked here at laundry, sewing and other labour, and some were punished with solitary confinement, hard work or shaved heads. Many arrived with children, and the death rate among infants was appallingly high. The factory is part of the Australian Convict Sites World Heritage listing, which includes eleven places across Australia that tell the story of the forced migration of convicts and the building of the colony.

Today the site is quiet, with the remains of the walls and yards, an interpretation centre, and dramatised tours that bring the stories of individual women to life. It is a sobering place, but also a moving one, as the descendants of many of these women now number in the hundreds of thousands, and the tours honour their resilience.

Just down the road stands the Cascade Brewery, the oldest operating brewery in Australia, its grand old building set against the forested slopes of the mountain. Above it, the road to the summit of kunanyi climbs through forests of eucalyptus and tree ferns to a height of over twelve hundred metres, with a series of tight bends and steep sections, and a view from the top over Hobart, the Derwent estuary and much of southern Tasmania. The weather at the summit can be bitterly cold and windy, even in summer, and snow and ice can close the road at any time of year.

Hobart, the capital of Tasmania, has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants, with a lively waterfront, the Salamanca markets on Saturdays, and the provocative MONA museum on the Derwent. Tasmania is a superb place to ride, with quiet roads, varied landscapes and very little traffic outside the towns. The road south to Port Arthur, the most famous of the convict sites, takes you through the Tasman Peninsula, with dramatic coastal cliffs. Watch out for wildlife on the roads, especially at night, when wallabies, possums and wombats are active.
t.port arthur historic site@-43.1,147.9:
At the end of the Tasman Peninsula, south-east of Hobart, the ruins of Port Arthur sit on a quiet green bay surrounded by eucalyptus forest, and it is hard to imagine a more beautiful place for such a grim history. From 1830 to 1877 it was a penal settlement for convicts who had committed further crimes in the colonies, a place of hard labour, harsh punishment and, later, a model prison where silence and isolation were supposed to reform the mind. The great sandstone shell of the penitentiary, the church, the separate prison and the houses of officials still stand in the grounds, and the boat trip to the Isle of the Dead, where convicts and free settlers were buried, completes the picture. Port Arthur is one of the eleven Australian Convict Sites inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2010.

The site also carries a recent tragedy. In 1996, a gunman killed thirty-five people at and around Port Arthur, the worst mass shooting in modern Australian history, which led to the country's strict gun laws. A memorial garden at the site remembers the victims, and visitors are asked to approach the subject with respect.

The ride from Hobart is a pleasure. The Arthur Highway crosses the causeway at Sorell and the narrow isthmus at Dunalley, then reaches Eaglehawk Neck, a strip of land only a few dozen metres wide where convicts trying to escape were stopped by a line of chained dogs. Nearby, the Tessellated Pavement, a natural rock platform cracked into neat tiles, the Tasman Arch and the Devil's Kitchen, sea cliffs carved by the waves, are worth a stop. The road winds through forest and along the coast with good surfaces and moderate traffic, but beware of wildlife at dusk and dawn: wallabies, pademelons and possums are often on the road, and roadkill is common.

The small towns on the peninsula have limited services, so fill up at Sorell before you go. There are cafés and a restaurant at the historic site itself, and the coast offers fresh seafood, especially oysters from the local farms. The weather can change quickly, with cold winds from the Southern Ocean even in summer, so bring layers.
t.human rights@-25.7,28.2:
Pretoria's Union Buildings stand on Meintjieskop, a low ridge looking over the city, and from the terraced gardens you can see the whole sweep of the South African capital spread out below. The sandstone buildings, with two wings joined by a curved colonnade, were designed by the English architect Herbert Baker and finished in 1913, to house the government of the newly formed Union of South Africa. For decades they were the seat of white minority rule. On 10 May 1994 they became the setting for the inauguration of Nelson Mandela as the first democratically elected president, and with that the meaning of the place changed.

That is why the point carries the label Human Rights. The Union Buildings are part of a UNESCO listing from 2024 on the legacy of Nelson Mandela and the liberation struggle, which links places in South Africa associated with the fight against apartheid and the building of a new constitutional order. A large bronze statue of Mandela, with open arms, stands in the gardens, and the view across the city from the terraces is a popular place for photographs, and for ceremonies.

Pretoria is also known as the Jacaranda City. In October and November the streets are covered in the purple blossom of thousands of trees, planted over a century ago, and the petals carpet the roads and parked cars. In the afternoon, summer thunderstorms often roll in with heavy rain and hail, so it pays to start early. Winters are dry and sunny, with chilly mornings, and the best weather for a long ride is from April to September.

The city is a good base. The N1 and N4 highways make for fast progress, and the surrounding countryside has rewarding rides: the Magaliesberg range to the west, the quiet back roads of the Cradle of Humankind toward Sterkfontein, where fossils of early human ancestors have been found, including the famous skull known as Mrs Ples, found in 1947. Constitution Hill, in Johannesburg, the old prison and now home of the Constitutional Court, is the other stop.

Fuel is easy in a city of this size, with stations on every main road. Like any large South African city, it asks for sensible habits: park in guarded places, keep valuables out of sight, and ask local riders about the areas to avoid. Then enjoy the slower side of Pretoria, with its cafes, its Dutch-Cape architecture and its very good steaks.
t.vilnius historic centre@54.7,25.3:
The old town of Vilnius is one of the largest surviving medieval centres in Eastern Europe, and its mix of styles, Gothic, Renaissance and above all Baroque, is delightful. The city lies at the meeting of the Neris and Vilnia rivers, and legend says that the grand duke Gediminas dreamed of an iron wolf howling on a hill, and was told to build a city on the spot in the early fourteenth century. Whatever the truth, Vilnius became the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, a huge state that once stretched from the Baltic nearly to the Black Sea, and later a centre of Jewish learning so great that it was called the Jerusalem of the North.

The old town has more than a thousand historic buildings, and some forty churches, among them the Gothic church of Saint Anne, a marvel of red brick, which, according to legend, impressed Napoleon so much that he wished to carry it back to Paris in the palm of his hand. The University of Vilnius, founded in 1579, has courtyards and arcades you can wander through, and the Gate of Dawn, with its chapel and a revered icon of the Virgin, is a site of pilgrimage for Catholics and Orthodox alike. UNESCO listed the historic centre in 1994.

The Užupis district, across the river, is a bohemian quarter that declared itself a republic on 1 April 1997, with its own constitution displayed on a wall in many languages, and artists and cafes fill the lanes. Nearby, the hill of Gediminas, with its tower, gives a view across the red roofs and church spires, and the whole old town is a labyrinth of cobbled lanes and small squares.

For a rider, the old town is for walking. Many streets are cobbled and slippery in the rain, some are closed to traffic, and parking is limited, so park outside the centre and go in on foot. Fuel stations are everywhere around the city, which has over half a million people. The roads leading out are easy and flat, with forest, lakes and farmland, and the ride goes to Kernavė, the ancient capital of the early Lithuanian state, on the Neris river, a landscape of mounds and old hillforts. Try cepelinai, large potato dumplings filled with meat, or cold beetroot soup in summer, with a glass of kvass.
t.sharpeville graves site b@-26.7,27.9:
On the morning of 21 March 1960, several thousand people gathered at the police station in Sharpeville, a Black township beside Vereeniging in what is now Gauteng, to protest against the pass laws that controlled where they could live and work. By early afternoon the police had opened fire, and sixty-nine people lay dead, many shot in the back as they ran. The massacre made headlines around the world, led to the banning of the African National Congress and the Pan Africanist Congress, and pushed the liberation movements toward armed struggle. South Africa now marks the date as Human Rights Day, and the graves of the victims in the nearby Phelindaba cemetery are part of the memorial landscape, together with the police station and a small museum.

It is a serious place to visit, and one best approached with patience. The cemetery is a quiet field with rows of simple headstones, and people from the community often come to tend them. Visitors are generally welcomed and guides, some of them with family connections to events, can tell the story with detail that no sign can give. Mandela returned here in December 1996 to sign the new constitution into law, a deliberate choice of ground.

The riding around is flat highveld, with straight roads, mine dumps, power lines and a lot of heavy traffic on the N1 and R59. It is not scenic in the usual sense, but the surrounding region has its own character, with the Vaal river a short distance to the south, offering lakes, weirs and weekend resorts. Drive carefully in the townships, where taxis stop without warning, and be aware that road conditions vary, with potholes after summer storms. Winters are dry and cold at night, and the afternoon thunderstorms of summer can be fierce.

Vereeniging, about four kilometres away, is a large city with fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and Johannesburg lies roughly an hour to the north. As elsewhere in Gauteng, personal safety needs sensible attention: park in sight, do not leave belongings on the bike, and consider arranging a local guide who can introduce you properly. Visit during daylight, dress simply and respectfully, and ask before taking photographs of people or graves.
t.tupischki tupishki@54.3,26.0:
Tupishki is a small place in the Ashmyany district of Belarus, a green and gently rolling country of low hills, lakes, farms and birch woods close to the Lithuanian border. The ride it belongs to is built around Mir Castle, the great brick and stone fortress that the Ilyinich and later the Radziwiłł families built from the sixteenth century on, and the whole of this region has a history of magnate estates, small wooden churches and the long, tangled story of the old Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

The nearest town of any size on the data is Halshany, about four kilometres off, and it has a ruined castle and a Franciscan church, built in the early seventeenth century under the Sapieha family, which was known for its large, handsome brick front. The wider landscape is of potato fields, hay meadows and storks nesting on telegraph poles, with villages of painted wooden houses with carved window frames. The light in late summer, low and golden over the stubble, is one of the pleasures of the country.

For riding, the secondary roads are narrow, flat and sometimes rough, with long straights between small villages, and tractors, carts and cyclists in the way. There is little crowding. Spring thaw leaves frost heaves and potholes, and winters are cold with snow lying for months, so the practical season runs from May to September. Distances between fuel stations can be larger than you expect, though main roads have decent coverage.

Belarus is a country that asks foreign motorcyclists to think ahead. Entry rules, visas, vehicle insurance and border crossings have changed repeatedly, and the situation with neighbouring countries has made land crossings difficult, so check the current rules with official sources before planning anything. Carry papers, keep to the speed limits, which are policed with cameras, and expect checkpoints. Halshany has basic services and fuel, but for a larger choice of food and lodging the district centre, Ashmyany, and the capital Minsk are better. Pastries and dumplings called draniki, potato pancakes, are the staple of most roadside cafés, usually served with sour cream.
t.the chocolate tablet breccia site@-26.9,:
There is a piece of rock in the Free State of South Africa that looks like a bar of chocolate. Look closely at the Chocolate Tablet Breccia and you see a grid of intersecting cracks, cutting the stone into neat rectangular blocks that really do resemble the segments of a chocolate tablet. It is a small thing, and also a very large one, because these cracks are a record of the shock that hit this land about two billion years ago.

That shock is the Vredefort impact, the biggest known asteroid strike on Earth. The rocks near this site were shattered, melted and shoved upright in the minutes after impact, and what you walk on today is the eroded centre of the structure, now called the Vredefort Dome and inscribed by UNESCO in 2005. Geologists come from all over the world to study it. You do not need any training to enjoy the visit, though a good guide, or at least a local geological map, makes it much richer.

The landscape is rolling farmland and low ridges, with grassland, maize fields and thorn trees, a quiet part of the interior highveld. Roads are mostly good tarmac, with long gentle curves and gravel farm turn-offs, and the surface can get rough near the dome. Traffic is light. Watch for livestock, and for minibus taxis, which stop and start without warning. In summer, afternoons bring thunderstorms; in winter, mornings are cold and clear.

Potchefstroom, a university town of about 120,000 people twenty-odd kilometres away, is where to fill the tank, eat and sleep. It is one of the oldest towns in the old Transvaal, with a good-looking centre and plenty of cafes. At the site itself, expect nothing but rock and a gate, and note that many of the places in the dome are on private farmland, so check access before heading off the main road.
t.the stromatolite basal fault plane site@:
Microbes made this. That is the surprising thing about stromatolites: the layered, domed structures that look like cabbages turned to stone are the fossil remains of mats of bacteria that lived in shallow water and trapped sediment, growing layer on layer. They are among the oldest evidence of life on the planet, and the rocks around the Vredefort Dome in South Africa carry some very ancient examples.

The site combines this with a basal fault plane, a surface where one layer of rock has slid over another. The two features give an unusual pairing, life at its earliest and violence at its biggest, since the dome itself is what remains of an enormous asteroid impact roughly two billion years ago. The area was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2005. Take the patience to look: the shapes are subtle, and a cloud passing or the angle of low sun can bring out the layers.

Riding here is easy and pleasant rather than dramatic. You are in the highveld at about fourteen hundred metres, in farm country of maize and sunflowers, with low hills and a huge sky. Tarmac roads run straight, then bend around koppies, and there is the occasional gravel stretch. Wind is regular, and afternoons in summer are often broken by sudden storms with lightning that is truly alarming, so stop and wait it out rather than push on.

For fuel, food and a bed, Potchefstroom is the closest large town, about seventeen kilometres away, with a long main street, student cafes and several petrol stations. Smaller settlements nearby may have a fuel pump, but opening hours are unreliable, so go into the country with a full tank. Much of the land is privately owned, so respect gates and fences, and ask before walking onto a farm. Spring, from September to November, with fresh grass and clear days, is a good season to go.
t.vredefort dome@-26.9,27.3:
A hundred and fifty kilometres from Johannesburg, the ground rises into a ring of low hills about seventy kilometres across, and that ring is the surviving core of the largest meteorite impact the Earth has kept a record of. Vredefort Dome formed about two billion years ago, when an asteroid several kilometres wide hit what was then a very different landscape. The structure was once perhaps three hundred kilometres across, and erosion since has scraped most of it away, leaving the central uplift visible. UNESCO listed it in 2005.

On the ground the effect is gentle and slightly confusing. There is no crater to stand at the edge of. Instead you ride across a landscape of granite domes and ridges, with the concentric hills of the collar rock rising around you, and the geology is knowledge more than view. Look for the steeply tilted layers in the ridges, which were flipped upright by the impact, and for the shatter cones, striated pieces of rock that formed in the shock wave. The nearby Vaal River curls around the north of the dome, and Parys, a pleasant little town on its bank, is popular with weekenders.

The roads suit a relaxed ride. Tarmac is generally good, with wide bends and long straights through farmland, and the gravel back roads are fine on a dual-sport bike when dry. Watch for stock on the road and for trucks on the main routes. Summer thunderstorms are fierce, and winter nights are cold enough for frost.

Vredefort, the small town after which the dome is named, is about twenty kilometres away and has a few services. Parys has more shops, places to eat and fuel, and Potchefstroom is bigger still. If you want to learn more about the science, try to arrange a visit with a local guide, because the best features are on private farms and are easy to miss. The light is excellent in the early morning and late afternoon.
t.western explorer highland@-41.4,145.0:
The Western Explorer Road is a long gravel track across the empty heart of north-west Tasmania, and in its highland stretches it passes through a landscape that looks like the surface of another planet. Buttongrass moorland rolls out in every direction, an orange-brown mat of sedges stained by tannins and burned by lightning in the dry years, with low ridges and quartzite outcrops sticking out like bones. There are no villages, no farms and, in many places, no trees, and the sky is huge.

The road was pushed through in stages over the late twentieth century to link the north-west coast with the west, partly to serve the mines and partly to open up the wilderness, and it still carries only a trickle of traffic. In wet weather the surface is slippery clay and standing water, and in dry weather it is dusty gravel with corrugations that can shake a bike hard. Riders usually choose dual-sport machines or well-set-up adventure bikes, and travel it with a little more patience than they would on tarmac. Rain can arrive at any time of year and with little warning, and the temperature on the plateau, even in summer, can be cold enough to need a thick layer.

The area lies on the edge of the Tarkine and not far from the Savage River, where an old iron ore mine and a slurry pipeline cut through the forest. The contrast between wilderness and industry is part of the story of the region, and the debates about mining and conservation here have been hard fought for decades. A short way down the road is Corinna, a former gold-mining settlement on the Pieman River, where a small barge carries vehicles across the water. It is a lovely old place with a handful of cottages and a cafe, but check the operating times of the crossing before you plan your day.

Wildlife is abundant if you slow down and look. Wedge-tailed eagles circle over the open ground, wallabies and pademelons graze on the verges, and in the quiet hours of dusk and dawn you may spot a Tasmanian devil or a quoll. They tend to appear on the road at the worst moment, so keep your speed modest.

Smithton to the north and Zeehan to the south are the practical stops. Carry water, tools, a tyre repair kit and some food, and let someone know your plan. It is a magnificent road for those who prepare for it, and an unforgiving one for those who do not.
t.richmond@-42.7,147.4:
Richmond is the Tasmanian village where the bridge is older than almost anything on the mainland. The sandstone arch across the Coal River was built by convict labour and completed in 1823, and it is the oldest bridge in Australia still in use. Cars cross it, cyclists wobble over it, and ducks paddle underneath, and standing on the grass looking at the weathered golden stone it feels as if the nineteenth century has simply been left in place.

The village sits in the Coal River valley, about twenty-five kilometres north-east of Hobart, in country that is dry by Tasmanian standards and well suited to vines. The soil and the sheltered climate have made the valley a respected wine region, with vineyards producing Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and tasting rooms are scattered along the roads around the village. For a rider, that is a temptation to be resisted until the end of the day, or at least to be resisted in quantity.

Richmond's convict history is vivid. The old gaol, built in 1825, is one of the oldest in the country and predates the much more famous Port Arthur by several years. It is still standing, with cells, a flogging yard and a kitchen, and a visit gives a sobering picture of how the convict system operated. Elsewhere the village has been kept in a tidy Georgian style, with sandstone cottages, a Catholic church that is among the oldest in the country, and a collection of tearooms and craft shops. It can feel a little like a stage set when the tour buses are in, but early on a weekday morning it is calm and handsome.

The ride in from Hobart goes across the Tasman Bridge and out through the eastern suburbs, joining the road to the airport and then taking quieter country lanes into the village. Roads through the valley are small, with gentle bends and open views, and with some care you can find a loop through the vineyards and back that takes in a few hills without any difficulty. Surfaces are generally fair, though some of the narrower lanes have gravel patches.

You will find a bakery in the village, famous locally for its pies and pastries, and several cafes and a couple of pubs. Fuel is thin on the ground in the village, so fill the tank in Hobart's eastern suburbs, around Lindisfarne, or in Sorell on the way to the east coast, and you will not have to think about it again. In autumn, the poplars and oaks turn yellow and the village looks its best.
t.oatlands@-42.3,147.4:
Oatlands sits on the Midland Highway in the middle of Tasmania, and it is built almost entirely of local sandstone. The main street is lined with Georgian buildings, shops, inns and cottages, many of them dating from the 1830s and 1840s, and the town claims one of the largest collections of such buildings in Australia. It is not a showpiece, and many of them are simply in daily use, as houses and cafes and a bakery, which gives the place its reality.

The town was founded as a military post, a stop on the road between Hobart and Launceston to keep order among the convicts and the bushrangers who roamed the Midlands. The convicts quarried the stone and built the buildings. The Callington Mill, a tower windmill of 1837, stands on the hill above the town, and has been restored and now operates as a distillery and visitor centre. The mill is a clear landmark across the dry landscape, with a cap that turns to face the wind.

The landscape of the Tasmanian Midlands is open, grassy and gently rolling, scattered with sheep and white-barked gum trees. It is a drier, colder country than the coast, often frosty in winter, and the weather can change fast. Lake Dulverton, beside the town, is a shallow lake that fills and empties with the seasons and attracts black swans and other waterbirds, and it has a nature trail and a small hide.

The Midland Highway itself is a main road, with long straights and gentle curves, and for a rider it is more a means of getting between places than a destination. Freight trucks use it, and there are overtaking lanes and speed cameras on parts. The charm is in the stops, and the old stone buildings make a pleasant break from the monotony of long, flat sections. Before leaving, take a short loop through the back lanes that lead into the hills, for a taste of country riding.

Oatlands is a good stop for fuel and food, with a pump on the main street and a few cafes, though hours can be short, particularly on quiet days. Bagdad, a small town about thirty-eight kilometres to the south, is the next place of any size toward Hobart, and Hobart itself is about an hour away. Try the local pies and, if you have time, a visit to the distillery, though with the bike outside it should be a slow one.
t.ross@-42.0,147.5:
Ross is a tiny sandstone village on the Macquarie River, and it is the prettiest stop on the Midland Highway. A bridge, a bakery and a few old buildings are all it needs. The bridge, built by convicts and opened in 1836, is one of the oldest in Australia still carrying traffic, and its arch is decorated with nearly two hundred carved stones, the work of two convict stonemasons, Daniel Herbert and James Colbeck, who were pardoned for their efforts. The carvings include Celtic symbols, animals, and portraits of figures from the time, and every face seems to have a personality.

The town's layout has a nickname, the Four Corners of Ross, because at the crossroads at the centre there stand a church, a hotel, a town hall and the old gaol, and locals describe them as representing salvation, temptation, recreation and damnation. It is a good joke, and the buildings are all handsome, in the warm local stone. Ross also has a Female Factory, a ruin of a convict women's prison, which is a sobering reminder of how the system worked. The nearby Midlands are the heart of the Tasmanian merino wool trade, and the sheep that graze the dry paddocks produce some of the finest fleece in the world.

The village bakery is the other reason to stop. It bakes in a wood-fired oven and is known throughout the state for its pies and its scallop pie in particular, and on a weekend the queue can stretch out the door. Eat one at a table outside, with the bridge in view, and the village will feel exactly right. There is a tearoom, a museum and a handful of shops selling wool and craft.

The road here is the Midland Highway, a fast route with straights, rolling hills and traffic, and from a motorcyclist's point of view it is not a thrilling ride. The best use of it is as a connection between more interesting roads on the east and west coasts. Take care in winter, when mornings are cold and frosty, and in summer, when kangaroos, wallabies and wombats stray onto the road at dusk. Bushfire risk in the dry months can lead to restrictions.

Campbell Town, to the north, and Oatlands, to the south, are the safer places to refill, and a tank topped up at either will see you through. The village is at its best in the autumn, when the poplars along the river turn yellow.
t.vadso@70.1,29.7:
Vadsø is the main town of the Varanger peninsula, and it feels like it knows it is on the edge of things. About five thousand people live here, on a low, treeless shore facing a fjord that opens straight into the Barents Sea, and the light off that water in summer is flat, silvery and long. It is the administrative centre of Finnmark, which explains the solid public buildings, and it has a harbour, a main street, a church and the sort of supermarket you start to appreciate when you have been riding the empty tundra for a day or two.

The town has a layered past. For centuries Sami, Norwegians, Russians and Finnish-speaking settlers known as Kvens traded and fished along this coast, and Vadsø became the centre of the Kven community in Norway. There is a museum devoted to their story, which is a good rainy-day stop. Out on the edge of town stands a mooring mast for airships, built in the 1920s when polar explorers like Amundsen and Nobile were using the north as their testing ground. Nobody has moored an airship there for ages, but it is a nice piece of improbable history, and it makes a good photograph against a pale sky.

The riding along this coast is long and open. The E75 comes in over treeless hills and wide plains, with distant fjord views, gentle curves and little traffic, and the surface is generally good. The main hazards are wind, which comes off the sea with no hills to stop it, and reindeer, which wander the road in summer and have no concept of right of way. Winter is serious, with snow, ice, darkness and sometimes closures, so only ride out of season if you have the kit and the experience. In June and July the sun stays up all night, and a ride at midnight is a real thing.

Vadsø has everything you need: fuel, banks, shops, cafés and a few hotels. This is the place to top the tank and buy food, because the next stretches are long and thin on services. The local fish is excellent, especially cod and king crab, which was introduced into the Barents Sea from Russia and now thrives off this coast. Try it, if you can, in a simple café by the harbour.
t.destrehan@29.9,-90.4:
Driving upriver from New Orleans, Destrehan is the first place where the old Mississippi plantation country comes into view, and it does so in a very ordinary way: between a refinery, a levee and a row of suburban houses. Then you see the long avenue of oaks, the white gallery and the deep roof of Destrehan Plantation, a house begun in the 1780s that is among the oldest surviving plantation homes in the lower Mississippi valley. It has been restored, and visitors can tour the house and its grounds.

The house was built for a planter, but the history around it is larger and harder than the architecture. The plantation grew indigo and later sugar, and it depended entirely on enslaved labour. In January 1811, enslaved people on plantations upriver rose in what is now called the German Coast Uprising, the largest slave revolt in American history, marching toward New Orleans before being put down by militia. The leaders were tried at Destrehan, and a number were executed. The site now presents this history in its tours, and it is worth listening carefully.

The Mississippi is the real organising force here. The river runs high behind the levee, sometimes above the level of the road, and ships glide past above the roofs of the houses, a strange sight. The land is flat, warm and damp, with live oaks draped in Spanish moss, cane fields and the occasional heron on a drainage ditch. The air smells of mud, cut grass and industry. The River Road follows the levee, sometimes beneath it, past plantation houses, small towns and chemical plants, and it feels at once historic and working.

The riding is flat and easy. The road is mostly smooth, with long straight runs, speed limits that vary through the small towns and the odd railroad crossing, and heavy industrial traffic near the plants.
