In summer the heat and humidity are fierce, and thunderstorms can arrive suddenly, so the cooler months from October to April are better. Watch for loose gravel at the edges, wildlife and slow vehicles.

Fuel, food and everything else are easy in Destrehan and Luling, which together hold more than twenty thousand people. Local cooking is Cajun and Creole, with gumbo, po'boys, boiled crawfish in season and bread pudding, and a cold drink on a shaded porch is welcome.

Give yourself time to walk under the oaks. The shade is real, and so is the history.
t.pretoria@-25.7,28.2:
Pretoria is South Africa's administrative capital, and it gets less attention than Johannesburg and Cape Town, which is part of its appeal. In October the city is painted purple by thousands of jacaranda trees, introduced from South America in the late nineteenth century, and the fallen blossom carpets the pavements. It sits in a warm valley under the Magaliesberg ridge, a little over fifty kilometres from Johannesburg, and its centre mixes Afrikaner history, colonial buildings and a lively black African present.

The Union Buildings, designed by Herbert Baker and finished in 1913, stand on a hill above the city with a famous view and terraced gardens. Nelson Mandela was inaugurated as president here in 1994, and a large bronze statue of him now stands on the terraces, arms outstretched. In the centre, Church Square has a statue of Paul Kruger and a set of imposing old buildings, while the Voortrekker Monument on a hill to the south tells the story of the Afrikaner trek in granite, a controversial but striking structure. The old Kruger House museum shows how the Boer president lived.

Rides from Pretoria go in many directions. North and east, the road leads toward the Magaliesberg hills, with their rock outcrops, dams and weekend retreats, and toward the Cullinan diamond mine, where the largest rough diamond ever found came from in 1905. Johannesburg and Soweto lie south, the latter reached on busy motorways such as the N1, which can be fast and dense with trucks and minibus taxis. Treat the minibus taxis with respect, as they stop and swerve without warning. The best months are April to October, dry and sunny, whereas summer brings short, violent afternoon thunderstorms, with hail on occasion.

Fuel is easy: petrol stations are everywhere, open at all hours on main roads, and attendants fill the tank, clean the windscreen and expect a small tip. Be careful about security in any large South African city, keep valuables out of sight, park in guarded areas and avoid riding late at night in unfamiliar districts. Food ranges from braai, the South African barbecue, with boerewors sausage, to bunny chow and Cape Malay curry, and the city's coffee shops are good places to rest before the road.
t.maloti drakensberg park@-29.8,29.1:
The Drakensberg is South Africa's great wall, a basalt escarpment that rises along the border with Lesotho for hundreds of kilometres and reaches over three thousand metres. The Zulus called it uKhahlamba, the barrier of spears, and the Afrikaners called it the Dragon Mountain. The uKhahlamba Drakensberg Park on the South African side and Sehlabathebe National Park in Lesotho together form the Maloti-Drakensberg Park, a World Heritage site recognised both for its landscape and for its remarkable collection of San rock paintings, some made by hunter-gatherers over several thousand years.

For a rider, the interest is the passes and the foothills. The roads in the foothills tend to be good tar, winding through green grassland, pine plantations and farmland, with the cliffs standing like a wall in the distance. The legendary route is the Sani Pass, from Himeville and Underberg up to the Lesotho border at roughly two thousand eight hundred metres, a steep, rough gravel track with tight switchbacks that is often attempted on adventure bikes in dry weather but can be dangerous in rain or snow. Check conditions locally, carry your passport, and be ready for border formalities. Snow can fall at any time of year at the top, and mist and storms build quickly. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms, winters are dry and clear but cold, and spring and autumn are probably the most comfortable.

The rock art is the secret treasure of the park. In caves and overhangs, the San people painted eland, the largest antelope, along with human figures, hunts and trance dances, using pigments from ochre, charcoal and animal fat. Some of the art may be more than two thousand years old. Access is usually through guided walks, which protect the paintings from damage, and visitors must never touch them. The wildlife is a reward too, with bearded vultures, Cape vultures, black wildebeest, rhebok and the quiet, reedy Berg streams where trout live.

Fuel is the thing to plan. The foothill villages are small, and the dependable stations are in towns such as Underberg, Winterton and Estcourt, so fill the tank before heading up. Carry water, warm layers, and a waterproof, because the weather in these mountains has a mind of its own. Lodges and campsites are plentiful in the foothills, and a night at one of them, with a fire and the great wall glowing at dusk, is an ideal ending.
t.underberg@-29.8,29.5:
Underberg is a small farming town in the foothills of the Southern Drakensberg, in the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands, and it is the last place of any size before the mountains. The little main street has a handful of shops, a pub, a few guesthouses and the scent of woodsmoke in the cool air, and above it all the Drakensberg escarpment rises in a wall of dark basalt. The district grows potatoes, apples and cattle, and the town has long served as a base for walkers and trout fishers.

It is best known as the starting point for the Sani Pass. The road, which climbs from Himeville and Underberg over the escarpment into Lesotho, is a gravel track that rises almost a thousand meters in about eight kilometers, with steep, loose hairpins and sheer drops. At the top lies the border post and the highest pub in Africa, at about 2,874 meters, which advertises itself with some pride. The pass was a smugglers' route and a mule track before it became a road in the 1950s, and it remains a challenging ride, especially in wet weather or after snowfall, when it can be closed. A capable adventure motorcycle and a confident rider can manage it in dry conditions, but the surface of rocks and ruts demands full attention.

Weather in the mountains changes quickly. Mist can form within minutes, snow can fall in winter and even on summer afternoons thunderstorms build over the escarpment. Temperatures at the top can be near freezing in the morning. The border post operates limited hours, and a passport is needed, so check the times before you go. Many riders leave early and return before dark.

The valley below the pass is good riding in its own right. Back roads around Underberg and Himeville wind through farmland and wetlands, and the views of the mountains are impressive, particularly in the light of late afternoon. Birdwatchers come for the rare wattled crane and bearded vulture, and trout streams run clear.

Underberg has a fuel station and basic supplies, and the nearby village of Himeville has a small museum and a pub. Fill up here before the climb, because there is nothing at the top beyond the lodge, and make sure your bike and tyres are ready for the rocks.
t.ukhahlamba drakensberg park@-29.4,29.5:
The Zulu name uKhahlamba means barrier of spears, and the first sight of the Drakensberg escarpment from the plain makes it clear why. For about two hundred kilometers along the border between KwaZulu-Natal and Lesotho, a wall of basalt cliffs rises to more than three thousand meters, broken by jagged buttresses, towers and deep gorges. The park protects much of it, and UNESCO gave it dual listing for both nature and culture in 2000, reflecting the richness of the wildlife and the astonishing rock art.

The paintings are the cultural treasure. San hunter-gatherers lived in these valleys for thousands of years, and left tens of thousands of images on the walls of caves and rock shelters, depicting eland, hunters, dancers and strange mixed figures that seem to show visions of trance. Some sites, such as those in the Giant's Castle area, can be visited with guides, and the paintings are best seen in gentle light. The San were eventually driven out by Zulu, Basotho and colonial settlers, and the last of them disappeared from the mountains in the nineteenth century.

For riders, the roads that lead to the mountains are among the best in the province. From the main road, long spurs run into the foothills, past resorts, farms and trout dams, and the views of the escarpment are grand in good weather. The pass at Oliviershoek, on the road to the Royal Natal National Park, climbs with bends and views toward the Amphitheatre, a cliff face about five kilometers long, over which the Tugela Falls plunge nearly a kilometer in several drops, among the highest in the world. Surfaces vary, and the dirt roads into the park can be rough after rain.

The weather is changeable. Summers are warm, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, and winters are cold and dry, with frosts and occasional snow on the peaks. Clear mornings are excellent, with crisp air and long views. Mist and cloud can descend quickly, so carry layers.

Fuel is available in towns such as Bergville, Winterton and Estcourt, but not within the park, so plan accordingly. Resorts and guesthouses along the foothills offer meals and beds, and an entrance fee is charged at the park gates. The great days here are the quiet ones, when the escarpment turns blue at dusk and the grassland smells of dry earth and wood smoke.
t.sani pass top@-29.6,29.3:
At the top of Sani Pass you are standing on the roof of the Drakensberg, close to 2,900 metres up, on the border between South Africa and the Kingdom of Lesotho. A small border post, a few huts, a stone chalet that claims to be the highest pub in Africa, and a view down the escarpment that makes your stomach lurch, are about all there is. On a clear day the plateau of Lesotho rolls away to the north, brown and treeless, while behind you the cliffs drop away into a haze of valleys.

The climb is the point. Sani is a gravel track, about eight kilometres of steep hairpins with a rise of around a thousand metres, and on the South African side it is open only to four-wheel-drive vehicles and good adventure bikes with experienced riders. The surface is rocky, loose and rutted, with stream crossings, and it turns treacherous in rain, snow or ice, which can come in any season. Mist often fills the gorge, and the weather at the top is cold and windy even when the valley below is warm. Passports are needed at both border posts, and you should check opening hours and conditions in advance.

The pass follows an old trade route used by Basotho traders and pack ponies carrying goods between the highlands and the coast. Its name comes from the San people who once lived here and left paintings in the rock shelters below. Later, a track for mule trains was improved for vehicles in the twentieth century, but it has never been paved, and that is its charm. On the Lesotho side, shepherds in woollen Basotho blankets and conical straw hats herd sheep and goats across the high pastures.

The landscape is dramatic and fragile. The high plateau is a cold, grassy desert with alpine flowers in summer, and wetlands that feed several of southern Africa's major rivers. Bearded vultures, one of the world's rarest raptors, nest on the cliffs, and the wind carries the smell of dry grass and woodsmoke. In winter, snow often closes the pass, and the chalet becomes a very cosy place.

Dress in layers, carry water and food, and do not attempt the ascent on a loaded road bike. Respect the border and the weather, and let someone know when you expect to return.
t.clarens@-28.5,28.4:
Clarens is the pretty one of the eastern Free State, a village of sandstone cottages, art galleries and tree-lined squares that sits at the foot of the Maluti mountains, with the cliffs of Golden Gate Highlands National Park on its doorstep. It was founded in 1912 and named after the Swiss town where the former Boer president Paul Kruger died in exile in 1904, a bit of Alpine nostalgia that suits the cool, bright air. Today it is a weekend retreat for people from Johannesburg and a handy base for riders, and the central square fills with tables on any sunny day.

The ride is the main draw. The road from Bethlehem runs west to east along the base of the Maluti range, through rolling farmland of maize and sunflowers, with the sandstone cliffs gradually closing in. Past Clarens, the road to Golden Gate climbs through a valley of amber and ochre rock, with towers and cliffs glowing at sunset, and the surface is mostly good tarmac with gentle, flowing bends. The weather can change quickly: afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and in winter frost and snow sometimes dust the peaks. Early morning and late afternoon bring the best light and the fewest cars.

The area has a long and layered past. San hunter-gatherers lived in the caves and shelters of the sandstone for thousands of years and left rock paintings that can still be seen in places. Later, Sotho and Boer farming communities moved in, and the region saw heavy fighting in the Anglo-Boer War, with campaigns fought across these hills. Dinosaur fossils have been found in the Clarens formation, a layer of sandstone that gave the town its geological claim to fame.

Nature is quiet and high. Black wildebeest, eland, zebra and springbok graze in the park, and bearded vultures and black eagles ride the updrafts above the cliffs. In late summer the grassland is a rich green, and in autumn it turns gold and rust, with the air smelling of dry grass and wood smoke. The village is also known for its small brewery and for its cafes, where a slice of cake and a strong coffee are an easy way to spend an hour.

Fuel is available in the village. Bring a jacket, even in summer, and book accommodation ahead on long weekends.
t.butha buthe@-28.8,28.3:
Butha-Buthe means place of lying down, and the name comes from the story of the Basotho people retreating to the flat-topped mountain above the town in the 1820s, when war and famine were tearing through the region, before their leader Moshoeshoe moved on to found his stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Today it is a lively northern Lesotho market town of a few thousand people in its centre, with a few more in the surrounding villages, set in a wide valley under steep brown mountains. It is the first real stop after the border crossing from South Africa, a short distance away.

For riders it is the natural first fuel and food stop in Lesotho, and a good place to get the feel of the country. The town has fuel, shops selling loaves and tinned goods, simple restaurants; carry a little local currency, loti or South African rand, for small purchases. The roads out of town climb into the mountains toward Moteng and Mahlasela passes, with good tarmac, long open bends and views across layers of ridges, though the surface can have patches of damage and the odd pothole. Livestock, including donkeys, goats and cattle, are a constant hazard, and so are minibus taxis stopping without warning. Weather in the mountains changes fast, and winter can bring snow, ice and fierce cold.

Lesotho is a country of mountain farming, and life here follows a seasonal rhythm. Men on horseback in woollen blankets pinned with large safety pins, and conical straw hats, move herds between pastures, and women carry water and loads on their heads. The blankets are not just clothing: they are a statement of identity and status, and patterns often carry meanings. The Basotho language has a rich tradition of poetry and song, and you will hear singing from schools and churches.

The landscape is high and open. Almost the whole country lies above a thousand metres, with a vast plateau cut by deep river valleys, and the highest peaks reach well over three thousand. Grass covers the slopes in summer, turning gold in winter, and the air is thin, bright and cold. Bearded vultures and black eagles soar above the ridges, and the rivers run clear over rock.

Carry your passport, vehicle papers and insurance for border formalities. Fill the tank in town, since the next stations may be a long way off, and dress warmly.
t.thaba tseka@-29.5,28.6:
Thaba-Tseka is the remote administrative town of the central highlands of Lesotho, a place that was founded in the 1970s to give government a foothold in the mountains and has the feel of a frontier outpost. The name means black mountain, and the dark ridge above town fits it. About five thousand people live here, in a scatter of government buildings, schools, shops and houses on a plateau more than two thousand metres up, where the air is thin and the nights are cold.

For riders it is a place of rare services. The town has fuel, basic restaurants, guesthouses and a few shops, and it is the last supply point on the long mountain road toward Semonkong and on the way to Katse Dam. The ride up from the north is fabulous: the road climbs over the high Mafika-Lisiu Pass, at more than three thousand metres one of the highest paved passes in southern Africa, with sharp hairpins, sweeping drops and spectacular views over the valleys. The tarmac is generally good but can have potholes and loose gravel, and ice and snow can close the pass in winter, so check the weather. The road south from Thaba-Tseka toward Semonkong is rougher, partly gravel, and a serious ride for experienced riders.

The history of the region is bound up with water. The Lesotho Highlands Water Project, one of the largest engineering schemes in Africa, built dams and tunnels in the 1990s and 2000s to send water to South Africa's Gauteng region, and Katse Dam, with its tall concrete wall, is the best known. The project brought roads, jobs and some controversy, and it explains why the roads here are better than you might expect. Meanwhile, daily life continues much as before, with herders moving sheep and Angora goats between pastures, and mohair and wool as the main exports.

Nature is high, bare and beautiful. The mountains are treeless, covered in grass and shrub, and in summer they are green with wildflowers, while in winter they are frosty and brown. Rivers cut deep gorges, and eagles and vultures circle overhead. At night, the sky is overwhelmingly full of stars, and the air smells of dry grass and woodsmoke.

Fill the tank and pack plenty of warm clothing, water and food. A spare tube, a tyre repair kit and a good map are essential, and it is wise to travel with another rider.
t.semonkong@-29.8,28.1:
Semonkong means place of smoke, and the name comes from the plume of spray thrown up by the Maletsunyane Falls, which drop nearly two hundred metres in a single leap into a gorge a short walk from the village. It is a small settlement in the mountains of central Lesotho, a place of stone houses, sheep pens and a handful of lodges, with a reputation among adventurous travellers that far outweighs its size.

The ride is one of the great gravel and tarmac mixes in southern Africa. The road from Maseru climbs steadily into the mountains, with long, winding bends, views across high, bare valleys and herders on horseback appearing round every corner. The surface alternates between good tarmac and rough, potholed patches, and the final stretches can be gravel or broken tarmac, depending on the year and the weather. Livestock, minibus taxis and children walking to school share the road, so ride with care. The weather is changeable, with sudden storms in summer and heavy snow in winter, so check the forecast.

Semonkong is known for its extreme activities. Pony trekking is the traditional way to explore the region, using the sure-footed Basotho ponies that have been bred for these mountains, and a guided ride to the falls or along the gorge is a gentle way to spend a day. A commercial abseil descends beside the falls and is promoted as one of the longest of its kind in the world, and the very brave tackle it. Visitors can also fish for trout in the cold streams, and winter brings a short season of snow.

The landscape is dramatic. The Maletsunyane river runs across a high plateau before plunging over the lip of the falls, and below the drop the gorge is deep and green. The surrounding hills are treeless, dotted with stone villages and terraced fields of maize and sorghum, and the light in the evening turns the grass orange. The air is cool and thin, and on a still night the sound of water carries a long way.

Fuel may be limited here, so fill in Maseru or at the last big town before arriving. Stock up on food, bring warm clothes, and be ready for a bumpy, memorable ride.
t.smithton@-40.8,145.1:
Smithton is the main town of Tasmania's far northwest, a farming and timber service town at the mouth of the Duck River, in a corner of the island known as Circular Head. With about four thousand people it is the last place of any size before the wild country west and south, and the land around it is gently rolling dairy and beef pasture, very green and often very wet. The air that blows in here has crossed the Southern Ocean with nothing in its way, and the Cape Grim station, not far off, measures it as some of the cleanest on the planet.

The district has an old, tough history. Timber cutters and farmers settled here in the nineteenth century, working for the Van Diemen's Land Company, which held enormous grants of land in the northwest. Nearby Stanley, with its flat-topped volcanic plug called The Nut, is a fine little fishing village with historic buildings, and it is worth a detour for a lunch of fresh seafood and a look at the view from the top. Cape Grim beef and local cheese turn up on the menus, and it is hard to go wrong.

Riders come to Smithton as the gateway to the Tarkine, the great wild rainforest region that spreads south and west. The Western Explorer is not a casual road: much of it is unsealed gravel, rutted and patchy, with corrugations, dust, and a lot of water when it rains. If you are on a big road bike with road tyres, think hard before you commit, and check the current state of the road before setting off. Keep the speed down, give yourself time, and carry a puncture kit.

Services are the big question. Fill up here in Smithton, because fuel is thin on the ground once you head into the Tarkine, and the next sure supply is far to the south. Buy food and water as well, and tell someone where you are going. The reward is a landscape of button-grass plains, tannin-stained rivers and dense myrtle forest, with the smell of wet earth and the chance of seeing a wedge-tailed eagle or a Tasmanian devil's tracks. Weather can turn cold and wet at any time of year, so pack rain gear and be ready for it.
t.corinna@-41.6,145.1:
Corinna is a place with a lot of history packed into very little space. A gold rush in the 1880s turned this bend of the Pieman River into a town of hundreds, with a hotel, shops and a stream of miners and timber cutters, and then the gold ran out and the people left. Today it is a handful of buildings in the middle of the Tarkine, one of the largest tracts of temperate rainforest in Australia, with a small wilderness lodge and a few cabins on the old townsite. The Pieman River is dark as tea, stained by tannins from the button-grass and the forest, and it moves slowly under the trees.

What sets Corinna apart is the river crossing. The road to the north crosses the Pieman by a small cable barge, nicknamed the Fatman, which carries a few vehicles at a time and runs during daylight, so check the times and have the fare ready. On a motorbike it is a gentle, slightly comic moment, standing with your helmet in your hand while the river drifts by. Beyond the crossing, the road changes character, and the gravel of the Western Explorer begins in earnest.

Around the settlement the forest is dense and mossy, full of myrtle, sassafras and the treasured huon pine, which can live for over a thousand years, and was once logged in the area. Cruises run on the Pieman toward the coast, where the river meets the sea at Pieman Heads, and the walks along the riverbank are gentle. The Tarkine's Aboriginal name, takayna, is increasingly used, and the area is rich with Aboriginal heritage, including ancient middens along the coast.

You should treat Corinna as remote. The nearest sizeable settlement is Zeehan to the south, a mining town with a mining museum, but the roads are long and slow. Mobile reception is unreliable, so tell someone your plan. In return you get a feeling of being properly far from anything, with only the sound of rain in the leaves and the creak of the barge cable to keep you company.
t.launceston@-41.4,147.1:
Launceston sits where three rivers meet, the North Esk, the South Esk and the Tamar, and the town takes its character from the water and the hills. It is Tasmania's second city, with something over a hundred thousand people, and it feels more like a large, well-kept country town than a metropolis. The Victorian architecture is excellent, because the city grew rich on wool, timber and mining in the nineteenth century, and the brick and sandstone buildings of the centre are among the best preserved in Australia.

The Cataract Gorge is the thing locals take you to see. It is a steep-sided slice of rock just a few minutes from the middle of town, where the South Esk runs down through a dramatic cleft, with walking tracks, a swimming basin and peacocks wandering across the lawns. There is a chairlift across the basin and a suspension bridge, and on a summer evening half of Launceston seems to be there. The city also has a long brewing tradition, with Boag's brewery going back to the 1880s, and a glass of the local lager goes well after a long day on the road.

As the finish of the Heritage Highway ride, the city is a pleasant reward. The highway, the old road between Hobart and Launceston, runs through the Midlands, a landscape of dry, golden hills, sheep country and stone bridges. It passes Ross, with a lovely convict-built bridge from 1836, and Campbell Town, with its brick-lined pavements, and Oatlands, with its old windmill. The riding is easy, with long straight runs and gentle rises, and it is more about history than adrenaline. A convict heritage is everywhere in the architecture and the roadside memorials.

Practicalities are easy. There is fuel on every corner, supermarkets, motorcycle dealers and a spread of hotels, so this is the place to sort out gear, rest and eat well. Tasmania's weather can change rapidly, even in summer, and Launceston has a reputation for chilly mornings and frost in winter, with mist lying in the valleys. Spring brings blossom, autumn brings gold in the trees, and almost any day brings a decent flat white.
t.varangerbotn@70.2,28.6:
Varangerbotn lies at the innermost point of the Varangerfjord in Finnmark, and it is a small place with a large role as the capital of the Sami culture of the east. The fjord is wide and cold, opening into the Barents Sea, and the landscape around is open tundra, low hills and scattered birch. The village has a Sami museum, the Várjjat Sámi Musea, which tells the story of the Sea Sami, who lived by fishing on the coast. Services are modest, and Kirkenes, to the east, and Vadsø, to the north, are the larger towns in the region.

The Varanger peninsula is far north and far east, east of Istanbul and Kiev at the same longitude, and the light and climate reflect that. In summer, the sun stays above the horizon from mid-May until late July, and in winter, the polar night lasts for weeks, though the northern lights compensate. The weather is cold and often windy, with fog from the sea, and snow can appear in any month except perhaps July. The tundra and fjord are a major stopover for birds, and Varanger is renowned for birdwatching, with sea eagles, eiders, puffins and many species of Arctic waders.

The Varanger National Tourist Route runs along the coast of the peninsula toward Vardø, with long, open stretches and views over the sea. The road is smooth and mostly straight, with gentle curves, and it passes through a landscape of bare rock and low vegetation. Reindeer are common, and there is also a strong chance of seeing white-tailed eagles. The surface is good, and traffic is very light. In winter, the road is closed or dangerous at times, and the best months are June to August.

Be prepared to be self-sufficient. Fuel is available in Varangerbotn at a small station, though opening hours may be limited, and it is best to fill the tank in a larger town. Food can be found at a small cafe and the museum, and local specialities include reindeer meat, cloudberries and fresh fish. In the evening light, the fjord is calm, and the stillness is deep. It is an unusual and rewarding start to a trip across the far north-east of Europe.
t.golden gate highlands@-28.5,28.6:
The cliffs here really do turn gold. Golden Gate Highlands National Park lies in the eastern Free State, in the foothills of the Maluti mountains on the border with Lesotho, and its great sandstone walls, layered in ochre, orange and cream, glow in the low light of morning and evening as if lit from within. The most famous formation is the Brandwag, a tall, isolated buttress that looks like a sentinel over the valley. Altitude ranges from about 1,900 metres to well over 2,700 at the highest points, so the air is cool and thin.

The park has a mix of grassland, wetland and sandstone ravine, home to black wildebeest, blesbok, eland, zebra and many smaller creatures, and it is one of the places where you can see the bearded vulture, a huge, rare bird of prey that nests on the high cliffs. Fossils of early dinosaurs have been found in the rock, and traces of San rock art can be found in shelters. A Basotho cultural village within the park shows traditional houses and crafts, a reminder of the people who have lived in these hills for generations.

For riders, the road through the park is a gem. The R712 winds between the cliffs and across the grassland, with long curves, sweeping views and little traffic, though you must slow down for animals and for tourists who stop to take photographs. Entry fees apply, and speed limits are enforced in the park, so be sure to ride at a gentle pace and respect the wildlife. Weather can change in minutes, with cold, mist and rain in the afternoons in summer, and snow possible in winter, so carry extra layers and waterproofs.

Within the park, there is a rest camp with accommodation and a restaurant, but fuel is not available, so fill the tank beforehand. The nearest big town is Phuthaditjhaba, about twenty kilometres away, with all services, and Clarens, a pretty village with galleries and cafés, is a short ride to the west. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times for the light on the cliffs, and the evening sky, far from city lights, is spectacular. Book accommodation in advance for holidays, when the park is popular.
t.bergville@-28.7,29.4:
Bergville is a small farming town at the foot of the northern Drakensberg, in the Okhahlamba district of KwaZulu-Natal, and its main role is to be a handy place to stop before heading for the big wall of mountains. The town lies on the Tugela river near the Woodstock dam, and on a clear day the escarpment rises on the western horizon in a long line of buttresses and cliffs, including the Amphitheatre, a rock face about five kilometres long. Behind it, the Tugela Falls, one of the tallest waterfalls on Earth by some measures, drops in several stages from the plateau of Lesotho.

The area has a long history of Zulu and Basotho settlement, and the rock shelters of the Drakensberg hold paintings made by the San people over thousands of years, which show animals, hunters and ritual scenes. The name Drakensberg, Dragon Mountains, is the Afrikaans one, and the Zulu name, uKhahlamba, means barrier of spears. Both capture the way the peaks look from the foothills, with spikes and teeth along the skyline.

The riding here is a gentle introduction to the mountains. Roads run through rolling grassland, farmland and small villages, with views of the escarpment on one side, and bends are easy and the surfaces are mixed, with good tarmac in some places and potholes in others. Cattle, goats and people on the road demand attention, especially in the afternoon, and thunderstorms in the summer can be violent, with lightning and hail, so keep an eye on the sky. Winter days are dry and clear, with cold nights and frost, and the light on the peaks is excellent.

Bergville itself has fuel stations, a couple of shops and basic services, and the supply is better than in the villages further up the valley, so use it. Winterton, a short distance away, has more shops and cafés, and several lodges and resorts in the foothills offer food and accommodation. A plate of grilled meat and pap, with a cold drink on a verandah, is a good end to the day. Bring warm layers for the evenings, even in summer, and book ahead during holidays.
t.mokhotlong@-29.3,29.1:
Mokhotlong is the remote capital of eastern Lesotho, a small town at about 2,200 metres where the road stops pretending to be easy. Its name is said to mean place of the bald ibis, after the rare, red-billed bird that nests on the cliffs in the area, and the town sits in a bowl of brown and green hills, with stone houses and tin roofs spreading up the slopes. In winter, snow often covers the highest ridges, and morning frost is a reliable companion, so riders should come prepared for cold.

The town is a trading post for the highlands. Shepherds ride in on Basotho ponies wrapped in thick woollen blankets, wearing rubber boots and the conical straw hat called a mokorotlo, and shop for maize meal, sugar and tobacco. The blankets, made in pastel and bold patterns, are a symbol of the country and a practical protection against the cold. Life here moves slowly, with a market, a hospital, and a few restaurants and guesthouses catering to the odd overlander.

For riders, the great attraction is the pass that begins above town. The Sani Pass climbs between Lesotho and KwaZulu-Natal, rising almost a thousand metres in a short distance on a steep, rough gravel track with tight hairpins, and the Lesotho side, where this ride starts, is the less frequently ridden direction. At the top stands a border post and a small chalet claiming to be the highest pub in Africa, at around 2,870 metres. You need a passport, the correct vehicle papers and sensible planning, and the pass can close in snow or heavy rain, so check conditions with locals.

Mokhotlong has fuel, though supplies can run short and prices vary, so fill the tank when you can, and carry some extra if your bike has a limited range. Food is simple and hearty, with maize porridge, stew, and fresh bread, and the people are friendly and curious. Roads beyond town are partly paved and partly gravel, and distances take longer than expected, so give yourself spare daylight. The Afriski resort, a small ski area in the north, shows how seriously the winter weather can be taken in these mountains.
t.moteng pass@-28.7,28.6:
Northern Lesotho is a country of high, treeless ridges and deep valleys, and the Moteng Pass is a good place to meet it. The road climbs from the lowlands near the South African border into the Maloti mountains, where villages of stone and thatch cling to the slopes and every hillside seems to be terraced with strips of maize and wheat. Phuthaditjhaba, a large town on the South African side about thirty kilometres away, and Butha-Buthe, the nearest Lesotho town of any size, are the points that anchor the region on a map.

Basotho life goes on beside the road. Herdboys in blankets watch flocks of sheep, goats and cattle, women carry water on their heads, and horsemen trot along on sturdy ponies that handle the steep ground with ease. The blanket, worn with a safety pin at the shoulder, is both clothing and a mark of identity, and the patterns are chosen with care. Most people are happy to return a wave, and the pace of life encourages riders to slow down and take it in.

The riding is exciting and demanding. Sections of the road are well surfaced, with sweeping views, but others are broken by potholes, loose edges and washouts, and livestock and pedestrians use the carriageway all the time. Ride well within your limits, avoid the road after dark, and do not underestimate the weather. At this altitude, cloud can drop into the valleys in minutes, and snow can fall in any month of the winter, even into spring, so waterproofs and a warm layer are essential, and a winter ride calls for heated gear.

Few places along the pass have reliable services. Fuel is available in the bigger towns, so fill up in Butha-Buthe or Phuthaditjhaba before you go, and carry water and food. Small shops in the villages sell basic supplies, bread, soft drinks and tinned food, and you may be offered tea in a home if you stop to ask for directions. Border formalities apply when entering Lesotho from South Africa, so bring your passport and vehicle papers. The best months are spring and autumn, when the air is clear and the hills are golden.
t.mahlasela pass@-28.8,28.8:
Few landscapes are as bare as these. In the highlands of northern Lesotho, there are almost no trees, because centuries of grazing and the cold climate have left the hills covered in grass, with rocks, streams and gullies cut into the hillsides, and the Mahlasela Pass climbs over this bare country in a series of long curves. The view from the top reaches across layer after layer of ridge, each paler than the last, until the horizon fades into haze.

The rock is basalt, the remains of enormous lava flows that poured out of the earth about a hundred and eighty million years ago and piled up to form the Maloti and the Drakensberg. Erosion has cut this basalt into stepped slopes and steep cliffs, and streams fed by snow and summer storms run through narrow valleys. This is the source of much of southern Africa's water, and the rivers that begin here flow toward the Indian and Atlantic oceans, which is the basis of the dams and tunnels that make Lesotho one of the continent's biggest water exporters.

On a motorbike, the ride is both rewarding and tiring. The road surface varies, with some good sections and others with broken edges, and the climbs and descents are long, so brakes and tyres get a workout. Mist, hail and rain can arrive suddenly, and the wind on the ridges is cold and sharp, so allow extra time and keep fuel and water in reserve. Shepherds with flocks and the occasional horseman give the road a human scale, and there is little traffic apart from minibus taxis, which stop without warning.

Phuthaditjhaba, about twenty-nine kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size and the place for fuel and supplies, and there is little in the hills apart from scattered villages with small shops. Take your passport and the papers for your bike, as the border posts take time, and carry cash in small notes. In winter, snow and ice make the pass a serious proposition, so spring and autumn are better, and the clear air and long light make for some of the finest riding in southern Africa. Set off early and aim to be off the high ground before the afternoon storms.
t.katse dam@-29.3,28.5:
It takes a certain nerve to build a dam in a country this steep, and Katse is the proof that it can be done. Completed in the mid-1990s as part of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, the dam is a thin concrete arch nearly 190 metres high that holds back the Malibamatšo river, creating a long, branching reservoir in the mountains of central Lesotho. Water from it flows through a tunnel of some forty kilometres to the Ash river in South Africa, supplying the Gauteng region, around Johannesburg and Pretoria, while Lesotho receives royalties for the water.

The road to the dam is one of the most spectacular in the country. From the north, it climbs over high passes, including the Mafika Lisiu Pass, which is among the highest paved roads in Africa, then descends to the lake through a landscape of bare ridges, gorges and deep blue water, with Basotho villages perched on the slopes. The road was improved to serve the project, so the surface is mostly good, though landslides and potholes occur, and mist can reduce visibility sharply. Sheer drops and few barriers call for concentration.

The reservoir changes the character of the highlands, with the lake stretching away in long arms between the hills, and the dam wall itself, a curved sweep of grey concrete, is impressive from the viewpoint. A visitor centre explains the history and engineering, and tours of the dam wall can be arranged. Some of the drowned valleys held villages and fields, and resettlement was part of the project, a subject that is discussed openly in the area. Birdlife includes the bearded vulture and the Cape vulture, which soar along the cliffs.

Thaba-Tseka, twenty-three kilometres from the dam, is a small town with fuel, shops and basic services, and it is the best place to stock up, though supplies can be limited, so do not arrive with a nearly empty tank. A lodge near the dam offers meals and rooms with lake views, and boat trips and walks can be arranged. At altitude, the weather turns quickly, with cold nights even in summer, so bring warm gear. The late afternoon light on the water and the mountains is worth waiting for.
t.maseru@-29.3,27.5:
Maseru is a capital that feels more like a country town with ambitions. It sits on the western edge of Lesotho, right on the Caledon river, which forms the border with South Africa, and the Maseru Bridge border post, just across the river from the town of Ladybrand, is the main gateway into the kingdom. About a hundred and twenty thousand people live here, and the city's name is said to mean place of red sandstone. It began in 1869 as a police camp of the British, who administered the Basutoland protectorate until independence in 1966.

The cultural heart of the country lies close by. The mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu, about twenty-five kilometres away, was the base of King Moshoeshoe I, who united the Basotho people in the early nineteenth century and defended them against enemies, and a visit to the flat-topped hill, with its ruins and view, is the best way to understand the nation's story. In town, the Basotho Hat, a large building shaped like the traditional conical straw hat, is a landmark and houses a craft centre where you can buy woven goods, tapestries and blankets.

For a rider, Maseru is a place to prepare. The roads leading south and east into the mountains are paved for some distance, then become rougher, and the best plan is to arrive with your papers in order, change some money into maloti, the local currency, which is tied to the South African rand and accepted alongside it, and check over your bike. Traffic in the city is chaotic, with minibus taxis stopping anywhere, so take care. The climate is dry, with hot summers and cold winters, and thunderstorms in the afternoons can be fierce.

Everything is available in town, from fuel and tyres to banks and cafés, and Teyateyaneng, a smaller town to the north, is also worth knowing. Eat pap and stew, or grilled meat, at a local restaurant, and keep valuables out of sight in crowded places. If you cross the border with a motorcycle, allow time for formalities, especially on busy days. From here, the road to Semonkong and the great waterfall climbs steadily into the highlands, and the temperature drops with each hundred metres.
t.maletsunyane@-29.9,28.1:
The Maletsunyane Falls drop about two hundred metres in a single unbroken ribbon, and they do it in a canyon so remote that the sound of the water is the first thing you notice. The river runs across a high plateau of grass and sandstone, reaches a lip of rock, and falls into a deep, curved gorge of dark cliffs, where mist and spray rise in the air. The village nearby is called Semonkong, which means place of smoke, a name that comes from the cloud of spray that hangs over the falls.

Adventure tourism has put the place on the map. A famous abseil, billed as the longest single-drop commercial abseil in the world, takes people down beside the falls on a rope more than two hundred metres long, and a few operators run pony treks to the gorge and surrounding villages. The Basotho ponies, small, sure-footed horses bred for the mountains, are the best way to see the highlands at a gentle pace. Evenings in the village are quiet, with woodsmoke in the air and the sound of dogs and cattle in the distance.

The road from Maseru is a long and rewarding ride. It climbs from the lowlands into the Maloti on a mixture of paved and unpaved sections, over passes with wide views of bare hills and deep valleys, and through villages where people herd animals along the road. The surface can be broken and washed out in places, so ride carefully and plan for a slow day. Rain can arrive at any time of year, thunderstorms in summer are violent, and winter frost and snow are possible, so pack for all conditions.

Nako, a larger settlement about forty kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable place, but services are modest. Semonkong has a basic fuel supply, at best, so fill the tank in Maseru and carry a spare if you can. The lodge near the falls and a few guesthouses provide meals and beds, often with a fire in the evening. Bring cash in maloti, a good torch, and warm clothes, and leave plenty of daylight for the return, because the road is not one for the dark.
t.sehlabathebe@-29.9,29.1:
Sehlabathebe is about as far from anywhere as you can get in southern Africa, and that is its charm. The national park, in the south-east corner of Lesotho against the Drakensberg escarpment, was among the first protected areas in the country and is high, empty and rarely visited, a plateau at nearly 2,500 metres of grass, wetland and sandstone outcrops. The name is often translated as plateau of the shield, and the surrounding hills do have a wide, rounded look.

Weathering has sculpted the sandstone into arches, caves and balancing rocks, and clear pools and streams collect in hollows, home to a small population of fish and many frogs. The park is a stronghold for the bearded vulture, as well as the rare Maloti minnow, a tiny fish found only in this part of the world, and its quiet trails, rock overhangs with San paintings and streams make it a favourite with hikers and anglers. Pony treks are available, and visitors tend to stay several days.

The road to get here is a serious undertaking. From Qacha's Nek, a border town to the south, the way runs over rough tracks and high ground, with deep ruts, washouts and river crossings, and from the north it is no easier. It is strictly the realm of experienced riders on suitable bikes, with spare tubes, tools and a plan, and it is wise to travel with others. Weather changes quickly, and mist, rain and snow can make the track impassable. Ask locally before you go, and expect to take much longer than the map suggests.

Fill up in Qacha's Nek or Matatiele before the long run, and add a reserve. The lodge and campsite offer basic accommodation, and the night sky is dazzling. Take warm clothes, a good map and a means of calling for help, since there is little mobile coverage. The reward is silence and a landscape few ever see.
t.nordkapp e69 point 3@71.2,25.8:
The North Cape is a cliff at the end of Europe, or so the tourist board would have it. In truth, the peninsula of Knivskjellodden, a little to the west, reaches slightly further north, and the mainland has points farther still, but the plateau of Nordkapp at 71 degrees north, a sheer 307 metres above the Barents Sea, is the place everyone comes to. A steel globe stands at the edge, and a visitor centre, partly carved into the rock, sits on the plateau with a restaurant and exhibitions. Honningsvåg is about thirty kilometres back down the road.

The last stretch of the ride is a long climb across bare tundra, with views of cliffs and sea on both sides, and the wind can be fierce enough to move a bike on its stand. There is a charge to enter the plateau, which covers the visitor centre and the parking, and in summer the car park fills with coaches, campervans and motorcyclists who have come from all over Europe to take the same photograph. Early morning or late evening is best, when the crowds are thin and the midnight sun lights the cliff.

The midnight sun here lasts from mid-May to late July, with the sun staying above the horizon throughout the night, and the long, low light is what people remember. In winter the plateau is dark and often closed by storms. The cliffs are home to puffins, kittiwakes and other seabirds, and the sea below is full of fish and the occasional whale. Fog is common, and it can swallow the view completely, so a clear day is a gift.

The visitor centre has a cafe and shop, and the food is expensive but warm. The road to the cape is open in summer, from about May to October, and in winter it is only passable in convoy and sometimes closed. Pack a warm layer and windproof gloves, because even in July the temperature on the plateau can be close to freezing.
t.sani pass point 2@-29.6,29.3:
The gravel begins where the comfort ends. Above Himeville the tar gives out and the Sani Pass road takes over, climbing along the valley of the Mkhomazana River toward the high wall of the Drakensberg. This is the lower part of the pass, close to the South African border post, and it is the stage where you find out how your bike likes loose stones, water crossings and ruts, before the real gradient starts.

The surface is the main thing to think about. It is rough, with embedded rock, patches of deep gravel and washouts after rain, and the road narrows as it goes up. Riders who know it set their tyre pressures lower, stand on the pegs and keep their speed modest, and the ones who get into trouble are usually those who try to ride it like a tarmac road. Four-by-fours share the track, and the sound of a diesel engine echoing up the valley is your cue to keep to your side.

The valley is lovely in a rugged way. Grassy slopes rise on both sides, dotted with proteas and the yellow flowers of the high grassland, and the first buttresses of the escarpment come into view ahead, dark basalt capped with mist. The Drakensberg is a World Heritage site, and the rivers that rise here feed much of KwaZulu-Natal. Look for rock hyrax on the stones and black eagles overhead.

Before you commit, there are formalities. The South African border post checks passports and, since you are heading into the Kingdom of Lesotho, you should carry your passport, vehicle registration and proof of insurance. Opening hours are limited, and the pass is not a place to arrive late in the day, because the climb takes longer than you would expect and the weather can turn quickly.

Fuel is not available here. Underberg and Himeville, a short ride back, are where riders fill up and where the last cafes and shops sit. Pack water, warm layers and a rain jacket, because the temperature drops sharply with altitude and even a summer morning can turn wet and cold.
t.sani pass point 3@-29.6,29.3:
Somewhere in the middle of Sani Pass the road stops being a track and becomes a staircase. The gradient steepens, the hairpins come close together, and the whole route zigzags up a face of rock that looks too steep for any vehicle. This is the section the pass is famous for, where the gravel is at its roughest and the views down the valley are at their most dramatic.

Riding it demands patience and balance. The corners are tight and often loose with stones, the inside of a hairpin can be rutted or scoured by water, and the edge on the outside has little or no barrier. Take each bend in a low gear with steady throttle, avoid grabbing the front brake, and if you need to stop, choose a place where you can put your foot down firmly. Many riders find that the climb is easier than they feared and the descent harder, because gravity is no longer helping you hold the line. Do not try to take the pass at night or in poor visibility.

The rock here is basalt, formed in an immense outpouring of lava roughly a hundred and eighty million years ago, when the supercontinent Gondwana was breaking apart. The layers show in the cliffs as horizontal bands, and in winter the water that seeps from them freezes into ribbons of ice. The air thins as you climb, and the sky takes on a deeper blue. Snow can fall at any time of year, and it is not unusual for the pass to be closed for a day or two in winter.

The road itself has a story. Long before modern vehicles used it, Basotho herders and traders walked and rode ponies up the same route, carrying wool, mohair and goods between the highlands and the coast. The first motor vehicles made the climb in the early twentieth century, and the track was later improved for four-wheel-drive traffic. It has never been tarred, partly because of the cost and partly because a smooth road would change the character of the place.

Carry water, warm clothes and a basic repair kit.
t.sani pass point 4@-29.6,29.3:
At the top of Sani Pass the ground levels off, and you are standing on the roof of southern Africa. The summit sits at around 2,874 metres, and the pass is the only road that climbs the Drakensberg escarpment between South Africa and Lesotho. The air is thin, the wind often sharp, and the landscape up here is open grassland and rock, without a tree in sight.

The Sani Top Chalet is the place most visitors aim for. It is a small mountain lodge that claims the title of the highest pub in Africa, and it has earned a legend for warming up frozen riders with a hot meal and a drink. Whatever you think of the claim, the chalet is a welcome sight after the climb, and the view from the terrace, which looks back down the zigzags and across the valleys of KwaZulu-Natal, is worth a coffee.

The border with Lesotho is here, and formalities take time. Both the South African and Lesotho posts need to be cleared, and you will need your passport, vehicle papers and insurance. Opening hours are limited, so check them before you leave and do not plan to arrive close to closing time. If the weather turns, the pass can be closed, and the border staff will tell you what to expect. Sani Top is where many riders turn around after a short visit, while others carry on into the highlands.

If you continue, the road toward Mokhotlong, around forty kilometres away, crosses high plateau country that feels like another planet. Basotho herders in thick blankets and rubber boots tend sheep and goats, and the villages are clusters of round stone huts with thatched roofs. Thaba Ntlenyana, the highest peak in southern Africa at about 3,480 metres, lies in the same range. The ground is often wet and the temperature low, with frost at night even in summer.

Fuel is scarce and unreliable in this part of Lesotho. Mokhotlong has some services, but it is wise to carry spare fuel if you plan to go beyond it and to keep your tank topped up from Underberg before the climb. Dress warmly, bring snacks and water, and allow plenty of time for the descent.

You are on Magerøya now, the bare island at the top of Norway, riding the final stretch of the E69 from Honningsvåg toward the North Cape. Behind you is the fishing town, ahead the cliff, and around you a landscape that looks almost lunar: rolling plateau of rock, moss and snow patches, no trees at all, and the sea visible on both sides. Reindeer graze here in summer, brought over by Sami herders, and they treat the road as part of their territory.

The road itself is a good one, about thirty kilometres from Honningsvåg to the cape, with long open curves, a few steeper climbs and some fine views down into bays. What makes it challenging is the weather. Fog can roll in off the Barents Sea in minutes, the wind can be strong enough to push a loaded bike across the lane, and even in July the temperature can sit in single figures. In winter the road is closed to free traffic and vehicles go in convoy behind a snowplough, so the riding season really runs from roughly May to September. Check conditions before you set out.

Getting onto the island was once an adventure in itself: until 1999 you needed a ferry. Now the North Cape Tunnel runs under the sea from the mainland, nearly seven kilometres long and dropping more than two hundred metres below sea level, with a steep climb out at either end. It is cold, damp and loud inside, and the descent can feel endless. The toll that used to apply was removed some years ago.

Honningsvåg is the last proper town, a fishing port of a few thousand people with fuel, a supermarket, cafes and hotels, and it is the place to fill up before the final run. At the North Cape itself, the clifftop plateau at 307 metres has a large visitor centre with a restaurant, a cinema and the famous globe monument, and there is an entry charge for the hall. The cape was made famous in 1553 by the English explorer Richard Chancellor, who named it while looking for a northern route to China, and it has drawn travellers ever since. Strictly speaking the neighbouring headland Knivskjellodden reaches a little further north, but it is only accessible on foot. For the midnight sun, aim for the cape between mid-May and late July, and pray for clear skies.

Vuonnabahta, Varangerbotn in Norwegian, is the small settlement at the head of the Varangerfjord, where the main roads of East Finnmark meet. The E6 comes in from the west and the south, the E75 heads east along the fjord toward Vadsø and Vardø, and it is a natural place to pause before tackling the long Varanger route along the northern shore. Around it the landscape is low and open, with birch scrub, bogs and gentle hills, and the fjord stretches away to the east, wide and grey.

This is Sami country, and the settlement is home to Várjjat Siida, the Varanger Sami Museum, which tells the story of the coastal Sami people who have lived around the fjord for thousands of years. The area is rich in archaeological sites, including old house sites, graves and traces of hunting and fishing communities going back to the Stone Age. The museum is a good introduction to the region and its people, and it is a modern building with exhibitions about language, culture and history.

The Varanger peninsula, to the north, is among the most remarkable landscapes in Norway, a high, bare plateau of tundra that ends in steep cliffs at the Barents Sea. It is famous among birdwatchers for its Arctic species, including king eiders and Steller's eiders in winter, and in summer the cliffs are home to huge colonies of seabirds. The road along the north shore of the fjord, toward Vadsø and Vardø, is the Varanger National Tourist Route.

The riding from here is open and atmospheric. The road follows the shore with long straights, gentle curves and wide views over the fjord, and the tarmac is mostly sound. You will rarely queue. Wind is a real factor and cold, and the sky rarely holds one mood for long. In summer the midnight sun gives endless days, and the light over the fjord and tundra is soft and golden. In autumn the colours of the tundra are extraordinary.

Varangerbotn has a shop and fuel, which is useful because services are sparse in this region. Tana bru, about fourteen kilometres away, has more options. Vadsø is the next town of any size, about sixty kilometres east.

Vadsø is the administrative centre of Finnmark, a small town on the north shore of the Varangerfjord with a distinctive history and a population of mixed origin. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, large numbers of Finnish-speaking settlers, known as Kvens, came here from northern Finland and Sweden, fleeing famine and looking for work in fishing, and for a time they were the majority of the town's population. Their heritage is still visible in the old farmhouses, the family names and the culture.

The Kven story is told in the Vadsø Museum, including the old Tuomainen farm, a well-preserved Kven homestead, and in a monument in the town centre that honours the immigrants. Vadsø also has a remarkable link to the history of polar exploration. On the small island of Vadsøya, connected to the town by a bridge, stands an airship mast that was used by Roald Amundsen's airship Norge in 1926, on its way to the North Pole, and by Umberto Nobile's Italia two years later. The mast is still there, a strange iron structure on a windswept island, and there are information panels about the expeditions.

Like the rest of Finnmark, Vadsø suffered heavily in the Second World War, when air raids destroyed much of the town, so most of what you see is post-war rebuilding with a few older survivors. Today the town is a modest administrative centre, with schools, offices, shops and a harbour.

The road along the fjord to and from Vadsø is part of the Varanger National Tourist Route, and it is a relaxed and open ride, with long views over the water and the tundra, gentle curves and good surface. Traffic stays thin. Gusts can be hefty and cold, and in winter the area is dark and stormy. In summer the light is endless, and the birdlife along the shore is rich.

Vadsø has every service a rider needs, so stop for a meal, a walk along the harbour and a visit to the airship mast. Kirkenes, only about forty kilometres away as the bird flies but much further by road around the head of the fjord, is the other main town in East Finnmark.
